item.content:encoded:
Chad Tracy has taken responsibility for the decision to pull Sonny Gray early in the Boston Red Sox's season-ending loss to the New York Yankees. Tracy said the move was his call after Boston fell 9-2 in Game 2 of the American League Wild Card Series.
Gray was removed with two outs in the fifth inning and Boston trailing 1-0. He had thrown 70 pitches and allowed two runs on six hits with five strikeouts before Erik Miller replaced him.
The decision drew attention because Gray had put together one of the best regular seasons of his career. He finished 18-5 with a 2.72 ERA, 149 strikeouts and a 1.15 WHIP across 29 starts.
Chad Tracy says pulling Sonny Gray in Game 2 was his call.
“The biggest thing, for me, coming into this, was dispelling any notion of people thinking that decisions get made prior to the game, or with a piece of paper, or with a computer.”
(Via: @NESN) pic.twitter.com/BPW9MTR4Av
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 5, 2026
According to Foul Territory on X, Tracy said the decision was his and that he wanted to dispel the idea that decisions were made before games through a predetermined plan or computer. His comments came after Gray openly expressed frustration with the early hook following Boston's elimination.
Gray said he wanted the chance to face Cody Bellinger for a third time through the lineup. He had held opposing hitters to a .180 average the third time through during the regular season, which was the best mark among qualified American League pitchers.
The decision became more difficult to defend when Miller allowed an RBI single to Bellinger after replacing Gray. The Yankees then broke the game open with a six-run sixth inning, turning a one-run game into a 9-2 victory and completing the two-game sweep.
Boston's season ended after a dramatic turnaround that saw the Red Sox recover from a 32-46 start and make the postseason. They finished 87-75, third in the AL East behind the Tampa Bay Rays and Yankees, before being outscored 18-2 in the Wild Card Series.
Tracy's explanation now provides more context for one of the biggest decisions of Boston's short postseason run. With the Red Sox eliminated, the focus shifts to the offseason and whether the club will continue with Tracy while determining Gray's future after a standout 2026 campaign.

item.content:encoded:
Six days after managing his first-ever postseason game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy sat in the Fenway Park interview room on Monday morning and answered perhaps the biggest question viewers had while watching the team be outscored 18-2 and swept by the hosting New York Yankees in last week’s Wild Card round:
Who made the call?
Specifically, who thought it best to pull Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray after just 4 2/3 innings in their respective Game 1 and Game 2 starts? Who thought struggling left-hander Erik Miller should relieve the starter not one, but both nights?
Was it the rookie manager, whose interim tag had been removed barely one week before the playoffs? Or was it chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and by extension, the front office, drawing up a pre-game road map for Tracy to follow?
“None,” Tracy said Monday. “The decisions are mine.”
Miller, the trade deadline addition from the Marcelo Mayer deal, had allowed earned runs in four consecutive appearances before a scoreless performance in his last regular-season game on Sept. 24. During that stretch, the 28-year-old southpaw openly admitted he was “working through some stuff.”
“Well, his last outing here at Fenway was exceptional, so he obviously fought it for much of September,” Tracy said, adding that Miller also had a “very good” extended side session before the end of the regular season. “Believe me, I see both sides. I don’t need to get too deep into defending this or that, because I certainly could have gone the other way with that, and that could have gone well, and we wouldn’t be having the conversation.”
Tolle’s pitch count was 83 after 4 2/3 innings of one-run ball. He struck out four, walked one, and yielded five hits in his first career postseason start. There were moments in which the rookie left-hander was grinding, but it was a 1-0 game and the Boston bullpen had lost several key arms to injuries, including righties Tyron Guerrero and Justin Slaten.
Tracy went to Miller after Tolle retired Yankees No. 9 hitter Paul Goldschmidt on one pitch. Ben Rice turned Miller’s third pitch into a solo home run. Though Miller only faced the minimum three batters before Tracy went to righty Greg Weissert, Rice’s homer was the dam-burster moment that led to a 9-0 Yankees win in Game 1.
With earned runs allowed in five of his last six appearances between the regular season and playoffs, it was even more stunning to see Tracy turn to Miller in nearly the same situation in Game 2.
Gray was on even better footing than Tolle, with 4 2/3 innings of one-run ball on just 70 pitches when Tracy went to the mound to take the ball. Though Gray allowed singles to Trent Grisham and Rice to put runners on the corners in the fifth, he also dominated the third time through the order all the regular season, holding opposing lineups to a .180 batting average and .515 OPS, and just seven extra-base hits in 162 plate appearances.
“I felt good, I felt crisp, I felt sharp, I felt like I was just out there competing,” a clearly-frustrated Gray said postgame. “I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact.”
“I would have liked to live-or-die with me in that moment,” Gray added. “I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment.”
Yet again, it was Miller who emerged from the bullpen. And again, Rice immediately scored to double the Yankees lead, this time on an RBI single by Cody Bellinger. The Red Sox ultimately lost 9-2 to end an even shorter playoff run than the year before, when they at least won Game 1 against the Yankees before dropping the remaining two.
With the entire Boston bullpen well-rested for Game 1, and all of the top arms available for Game 2 after not pitching in the series opener, doubling down on Miller seemed baffling that it could only be a decision handed down from the powers-that-be.
But not according to Tracy.
“We have information, just like all the other 29 teams have information,” Tracy said. “I’ve said this before, since I’ve been here, do I sit in the office and talk through … who’s available today? What’s the best way to deploy them? Who’s down? Every single day, you do that.
“But not one time since I’ve been here has anybody scripted a game, has anybody told me, ‘Use this number right here to decide in this inning.’ Those decisions, they’re mine. So as far as that specific one (to pull the starter), my decision, that obviously didn’t go great. That falls on me.”
Tracy added: “Do we have data analytics? Of course we do, everybody does. Is somebody standing there, pushing me, saying, ‘You need to do this, this and this? Absolutely not.”
Tracy in the hour-long press conference again refuted that he was forced into those pitching changes by anyone else and said “the biggest thing for me coming into this was, maybe dispelling any notion of people thinking that decisions get made prior to the game, or with a piece of paper or with a computer.”
“I do trust Sonny Gray, I do trust the guys in the bullpen as well,” Tracy said. “I think the easiest way to say it is like, it was my call. It was my decision. It went south. Here we are.”

Red Sox Nation left the Wild Card round with more questions than answers after being embarrassed by the Yankees. Following the Game 2 loss, fans were left heavily questioning manager Chad Tracy's decision-making, especially with regard to his management of the bullpen. The quotes that followed the game didn't help his case.
The moment that really got fans riled up was following Sonny Gray's departure in the fifth inning. With two outs and runners on first and third, Tracy handed the ball to Erik Miller in relief. In Game 1, Tracy did the same thing when taking Payton Tolle out in the fifth inning, and Miller immediately gave up a left-on-left home run. In Game 2, with lefty Cody Bellinger at the plate, the scuffling (regressing?) Miller allowed an RBI single, giving New York a 2-0 lead.
Fans were rightfully upset by the decision to trust Miller again. Not only had the lefty struggled down the stretch in the regular season, but he'd just shown the game before that just didn't have it. In the postgame press conference, Tracy tried to justify his move.
Chad Tracy only made himself look worse with his reasoning to use Erik Miller in Game 2 of the Wild Card
"I think, where we were at in today's game, we pretty clearly knew who we were going to throw," Tracy said in response to being asked about bringing on a lefty to face Bellinger, who hits lefties well. "Those are the best ones we have to offer, so it was pretty obvious we were going to be aggressive..."
What it sounds like Tracy is referencing is a game script. That if the Sox were at a certain point in the game, with a certain score, it was predetermined that Erik Miller was going to be the man called upon.
That was exactly what Willson Contreras was talking about in his postgame comments. The veteran first baseman lamented the Sox approach to the games, saying they relied too heavily on analytics and didn't have any feel for the flow of the game.
You can add Sonny Gray's comments in here, too. He mentioned hoping for more trust in the moment he was pulled from the game. He also talked about being one of the best pitchers this season when facing a lineup for the third time (which was true). Anyone who's followed baseball recently knows that analytics-heavy teams don't like pitchers facing a lineup for the third time.
What happened in the game, plus the quotes after, has left Red Sox fans scratching their heads as to what changed. In the middle of the season, it felt like the whole team was running on feel for the game. They pinch-hit in the perfect moments, even if it didn't feel right. They would allow pitchers to work through jams on trust.
Now, Red Sox Nation heads into the offseason questioning the ability of their newly extended manager. They are questioning how much autonomy he actually has from the front office. These questions are going to loom over the entire offseason and into next season.

The Boston Red Sox have turned their eyes to the offseason.
It’s earlier than they would’ve liked, but they were swept out of the AL Wild Card Series by the New York Yankees, and so now they’ve got to think about what the 2027 campaign will look like.
There’s one area where the Red Sox have the potential to be particularly busy in the offseason — whenever it can begin in earnest after a potential lockout — and that’s salary arbitration.
They’ll have a whopping 17 players up for salary arbitration, if they choose to tender them contracts.
One of the biggest names on that list is Wilyer Abreu, and MLB Trade Rumors writer Matt Swartz has projected values for all the Boston arbitration eligible players.
For Abreu, the number comes out to be quite the bargain.
Wilyer Abreu Contract Projection
The MLBTR projection for Abreu’s salary for the 2027 season comes in at $4.6 million.
For a player with the power, glove and throwing arm of Abreu, it certainly seems like a massive bargain.
That doesn’t consider everything that goes into arbitration, though.
Each player that reaches the major leagues via the minor leagues has six years of club control once they reach the majors.
The first three years have a salary based on the collective bargaining agreement, and they’re considered the pre-arbitration years.
Years four through six of a player’s time with a team are the arbitration years. In each of those offseasons, a player is eligible to go to salary arbitration to determine what he’s paid the following season.
The arbitration process features the team submitting a value and the player submitting one, and the independent arbitrator comes to a conclusion on which one wins out.
Teams and players these days often negotiate in advance to avoid actually going to what can be a contentious hearing, but the value they come out with will still end up close to what it would’ve been in arbitration.
All that said, it matters which year a player is in for the sequence — and this is only Abreu’s first arbitration year. Generally, the first arbitration year comes with the lowest salaries, and they rise in each of the two subsequent years, even if the player is viewed as having exactly the same value each season.
So for Abreu, no matter what he did this season, he wasn’t going to end up with a giant arbitration value.
The Red Sox could always look to give him a higher-paying contract extension and buy out some of his eventual free agent years, but for now, Abreu is headed for arbitration.
Other Red Sox in Arbitration
The list of 17 Red Sox heading to salary arbitration is long.
The full list is: Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, Adley Rutschman, Jarren Duran, Eli White, Kutter Crawford, Connor Wong, Romy Gonzalez, Triston Casas, Andruw Monasterio, Zack Kelly, Greg Weissert, Wilyer Abreu, Erik Miller, Justin Slaten, Jahmai Jones and Tyron Guerrero.
If a team chooses not to tender a player a contract, they instead go right to free agency.

item.content:encoded:
Baseball is a game of numbers. It’s played on the field, with balls and bats and gloves, but every action, decision, and outcome is measured by a number. Those numbers are presented to us during broadcasts, in gambling ads, and by people like me on Twitter and in pieces here on OTM. Most of the numbers we see are presented without context.
Just this week, there was plenty of chatter about how Payton Tolle has reverse splits and performs better against righties than he does against lefties. If you say that Tolle stats against righties are superior to those against lefties, you are correct. If you claim that opponents should start lefties against Tolle for that reason, citing that stat as evidence, you’d be a little bit off base.
In short, Tolle’s stats against lefties were worse than those against righties because he only throws to the best left-handed hitters. If he faced a lineup of nine lefties, he’d rack up strikeouts and groundball outs because of the pitches he has at his disposal. Tolle isn’t the point of this piece, though, so I digress.
Another example of this came after the final game of the season. The Red Sox bullpen got caved in by the Yankees, and the season ended in embarrassing fashion. During the postmortem, Sonny Gray, who was pulled after just 4.2 innings and 70 pitches, expressed his displeasure at not being allowed to continue. He said that he’s the best pitcher in the American League at facing a lineup for a third time.
His numbers facing hitters for a third time are in fact excellent: .515 OPS against, 21.6% strikeout rate, 6.8% walk rate, and a .180 batting average in 162 plate appearances across 28 games this season. Despite this, Gray wasn’t allowed to see Cody Bellinger for a third time; Erik Miller came in and gave up a run, and the game snowballed from there, ending the Red Sox season.
If you read my work, you know I like numbers. I do my best to provide context and try to blend the stats with on-field applications, but I admit that I tend to believe what the numbers say even if they go against conventional wisdom. Those choices that go against conventional wisdom have come to be known as “analytics”. If people don’t agree with something, they blame “analytics” without knowing what information was actually used in that decision.
In this case, the consensus was that Gray was removed because “analytics” say that seeing a lineup for the third time is a disadvantage. The numbers presented above disagree with that sentiment, but the Boston Red Sox, who pay people to research these types of things, aren’t making decisions based on slash lines in 150 plate appearance samples. Still, the decision was, at least in some part, motivated by statistics.
This piece is not in defense of Chad Tracy, Craig Breslow, or anyone else who might have had a hand in the decision-making process or game planning. In fact, I’ll go as far as to say that I staunchly disagree with the decision. I didn’t have a suite of statistics at my disposal at the time, but I thought Gray had a better chance of getting the out than Miller. I actually messaged the rest of the OTM staff and said: “So this is insane, right?” Before the game, I published a piece on how the Red Sox needed Sonny Gray to go deep into the game, for the sake of both Game 2 and a potential Game 3. Even after looking at the numbers that I’ll share momentarily, I disagree with the decision, although that’s easy to do in hindsight.
Instead of supporting or tearing down the decision, what I’m trying to do here is reverse-engineer the thought process and provide some context, because despite what sports talk radio or faceless Twitter accounts might tell you, it is much more nuanced than “third time through the order bad”. Let’s do it.
I’ll set the scene. It’s the fifth inning with the Yankees leading, 1-0. Trent Grisham has reached on a single to start the inning, and swapped places on the bases with Austin Wells, who grounded out to second base but beat the throw from Trevor Story to break up the double play. Ryan McMahon struck out on a good sweeper, and Ben Rice singled on a hard ground ball through the infield to move Wells up to third base. After 70 pitches and one earned run, Gray walked off the mound.
The first thing I’ll look at is Bellinger’s other at-bats against Gray. In his first trip to the plate, he roped a first-pitch sinker to Nick Sogard, who made a great pick to get the out. His second time up, he grounded out again, this time after fouling off three two-strike pitches and spitting on a good sweeper to his back foot. If you’re judging based on those two matchups alone, I could understand the decision to not give Bellinger a third crack at Gray. Bellinger looked like he was seeing the ball well.
Next, let’s look at how Gray approached the lineup to that point.
Against the eight lefties in the Yankees’ lineup, Gray used his four-seam and sinker a combined 59% of the time. The rest of his arsenal was made up of 12 sweepers, 10 curveballs, and three changeups. The fastballs were in the zone (~60% zone rate on both the four-seam and the sinker), while all three of his secondary pitches returned zone rates between 20% and 33%. While that might seem intuitive — fastballs in the zone, putaway pitches below it — that’s not always the case for Gray. He’s usually willing to flip his curveball in for called strikes, and occasionally does the same with his sweeper. On Wednesday, the plan was clearly to attack with fastballs for strikes, and breaking balls below the zone.
The Yankees’ lefties had the second-highest hard-hit rate against in-zone breaking balls from righties this season, as well as the seventh-highest barrel rate. They had the second-highest whiff rate, but Gray’s breaking balls didn’t miss bats in the zone this season. With those statistics in mind, it’s likely that Gray wasn’t going to change his game plan.
Now let’s look at the fastballs. The third time through the lineup, their performance seriously suffers. Entering the postseason, he threw his four-seam and sinker each about 18% of the time. He also used his cutter 15% of the time, but didn’t throw a single cutter to lefties on Wednesday and used it sparingly in his final start of the regular season, so it appeared to be removed from his game plan. The fastballs that he did use weren’t nearly as effective as they were early in games. The shape and velocity held, but the results did not. His four-seam ideal contact rate jumped from 40% to 56%, as the pitch found the middle of the plate often.
The sinker returned weak contact, but that was likely because the zone rate dropped from 60% the first two times through to 40% the third time through. Because of this, the called strike rate plummeted, and the strike rate fell to near 50%.
His breaking stuff wasn’t much better. The curveball had a huge swinging strike rate and chase rate, but when hitters did connect, it was hammered to the tune of a 67% ideal contact rate. The sweeper, his best whiff pitch, saw its chase rate drop 15% the third time through, thanks to bigger misses off the plate.
Bellinger is an excellent breaking ball hitter. Gray’s fastballs lose effectiveness later in games, and hitters don’t expand the zone as frequently against his sweepers. If those are your cards, you probably want to fold that hand in favor of another. The card that Tracy chose to play is a whole other can of worms, but there was a case for Gray to be removed.
If you read this and thought, “the analytics have gone too far, who cares that Gray’s sweeper is less effective the third time through the order it’s playoff baseball you pitch with your nuts not your arm blah blah blah”, I don’t blame you. As I wrote this, I questioned if I was too in the weeds myself, and still would have probably rolled the dice with Gray. Regardless of whether you agree or disagree with Gray’s early exit, I hope this provided some insight into what the team might have been thinking, because it really is deeper than blanket truths discovered by “analytics” that have been parroted 1,000 times by people who think Billy Beane ruined baseball.

The Boston Red Sox's 2026 campaign officially came to a close on Wednesday night, as they suffered a 9-2 loss at the hands of the New York Yankees in Game 2 of their wild-card series. Once again, the Sox got virtually no production on offense, while their bullpen fell apart down the stretch thanks to a bevy of head-scratching moves from manager Chad Tracy.
The most consequential decision from Tracy was his controversial decision to remove Sonny Gray from the game after 4.2 innings of work in favor of Erik Miller, who had just given up a crucial home run in Game 1 of this series the day before. Gray made it very clear after the game that he was not a fan of Tracy's decision to pull him, and it seems like All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras agrees with his teammate.
Willson Contreras Makes Thoughts Clear on Chad Tracy's Sonny Gray Move
In Game 1 against the Yankees, Tracy removed Payton Tolle after 4.2 innings of work and turned to Miller to face Ben Rice. Tolle was at 83 pitches on the night, but he had generally pitched well. The move immediately backfired, as Miller gave up a solo home run to Rice that woke up the rest of New York's lineup.
Tracy's decision to remove Gray in Game 2 was even more jarring, though. While a pair of runners were on first and second base, Gray had largely cruised through his outing, and this time, he was only at 70 pitches on the night. Tracy once again went to Miller out of the bullpen, and he quickly got burned again, with Miller giving up an RBI single to Cody Bellinger.
Gray did not hold back after the game when discussing Tracy's decision to pull him, saying he would have liked to be trusted in that situation after putting together such a successful season with the team. When asked about Tracy pulling Gray out of the game prematurely, Contreras didn't say anything, and instead pantomimed himself zipping his mouth shut and throwing away the key.
Red Sox Finish 2026 Campaign With Dispiriting Series vs. Yankees
So much went right for the Red Sox in their mid-summer turnaround that resulted in them finding their way to the postseason. At the end of the day, though, this team's weaknesses were too much to overcome. The lineup, which has been a weakness all year, did nothing aside from a pair of solo home runs from Contreras and Nick Sogard in Game 2, the bullpen faltered, and the lights were clearly too bright for Tracy, as every single move he made proved to be the wrong one.
Boston finds itself in the same exact spot it was in last offseason, as it clearly needs to make sweeping upgrades to its lineup in order to take the step forward it appears capable of taking. You'd think the front office would have figured this out after being subjected to the same fate in last year's playoffs, but if it puts together another weak offseason of work, the Red Sox could quickly find themselves stuck in the purgatory of being a consistently mediocre team.

The Boston Red Sox and Jarren Duran have been involved in swirling trade rumors for a while now.
Essentially all of last offseason was spent with the premise that the Red Sox had too many outfielders and that one was bound to get traded.
That never came to fruition, though, and so Duran remained in Boston for the 2026 season.
He struggled mightily, batting just .207 with limited power, and so questions will arise again.
The Red Sox still have the same amount of outfielders. Duran might not be worth as much, but he also might not be as crucial for Boston to keep around.
A year later, could a trade materialize?
That’s one question being asked as the Red Sox enter their offseason after being swept in two games in the AL Wild Card Series by the rival New York Yankees.
There are big questions for the sport of baseball to answer as a whole this winter. In Boston, though, Duran is going to be one of the biggest things to solve, one way or another.
Jarren Duran Trade Plans
ESPN’s David Schoenfield wrote about this question almost immediately following the Red Sox season ending, and he seems to arrive at the conclusion that a trade could definitely be coming.
“That leaves trading Duran on the agenda,” Schoenfield writes. “Roman Anthony’s nearly four-month stint on the IL meant the four-outfielders-for-three-positions problem never actually turned into a problem, but after hitting just .207/.266/.361, Duran is clearly fourth on the depth chart. His trade value took a nosedive, but he still somehow has two years left of team control, and the Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.”
There is certainly value for an acquiring team in the fact that Duran still has two more years under contract. Especially considering what a shortened season might do to player value, a team knowing it would also have Duran for 2028 could be appealing to anyone who still believes in his talent.
There may not be a lot of suitors, but Schoenfield writes that the “Red Sox will find a team willing to take a chance on him.” It’ll just be up to Boston at that point to follow through on the deal.
Why Red Sox Offseason Might Be Slow Otherwise
Aside from Duran, Schoenfield doesn’t think Boston will be very busy. They’ve already taken care of a bunch of things.
“While the Red Sox had a revolving door at shortstop and second base in 2026 — six different players started at short and seven at second — those positions will probably be resolved in 2027 with top prospect Franklin Arias and Curtis Mead, the trade deadline acquisition the Red Sox were going to play at second base until he got injured his first game with the team,” Schoenfield writes. “Trevor Story still has one more year left on his contract, but there’s no reason he should be playing ahead of Arias next season.”
Schoenfield also references the recent trades for Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Erik Miller as limiting the need for moves, since those guys all are under contract still.
His only other question: Does Sonny Gray retire, or return, or neither? The Red Sox still have things to figure out, just maybe not as much as some years.

Having been in the big leagues since 2013, Sonny Gray has accumulated a lot of stats in his career. He certainly can't be aware of all of them, but there's one this year that he clearly knew by heart.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time," Gray said Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium, after the Boston Red Sox were swept out of the Wild Card Series against the rival New York Yankees. "I think that's a fact."
Indeed, the 36-year-old was great when facing a lineup for a third time this year, holding hitters to a .180 average while posting a 1.99 ERA.
Yet, while the crafty veteran was aware of his effectiveness the third time through the batting order, his manager was either unaware or not interested in letting Gray pitch out of a miniature jam with Boston's season on the line.
After Gray allowed two singles with the Yankees leading 1-0 in the fifth, first-year manager Chad Tracy strode to the mound and inexplicably called upon lefty reliever Erik Miller for the second straight night at the same exact point in the game.
That move backfired immediately in Game 1, when Miller replaced Payton Tolle and surrendered a home run on his third pitch. And it failed again in Game 2, with Miller giving up two hits to the only batters he faced. The first was Cody Bellinger, who ripped an RBI single off Miller's slider to double the Yankees' lead to 2-0.
Gray, who will finish in the top three of AL Cy Young voting this year, felt he should have been given the chance to at least finish the fifth inning.
"I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. I think you could probably ask the guys, and they felt the same way," Gray said. "I felt strong, I felt confident, I felt convicted. But what can you do?"
Gray added: "I would have liked to been trusted in that moment."
Certainly, Gray's work both this season and throughout his career earned him a start in the playoffs over Ranger Suarez, who's one of the best postseason pitchers in baseball history. And at just 70 pitches, and after getting proper rest down the stretch, Gray was far from being on the ropes when Tracy made his call.
More Red Sox Coverage
Even though the decision to go to Miller allowed the Yankees to instantly double their leads in both games of the sweep, Tracy defended his decisions.
"[Tolle and Gray] are great, yeah. Our bullpen's been great all year, too," Tracy said. "It's a case sometimes of depending on what the score is and how much wiggle room we have, if we were able to put up some runs and maybe have some more breathing room, we might be able to [keep the starters in the game]. But trying to be aggressive and create tough matchups, and it just didn't work out."
Tracy's assertion that the bullpen has been great all year is true overall, but it doesn't apply to Miller specifically.
After joining the Red Sox as the return in the Marcelo Mayer trade, Miller made a strong first impression, posting a 0.63 ERA and 1.047 WHIP in his first 14 appearances. He struck out 25 batters and walked just six in that span, earning a trusted spot for high-leverage, late-game situations for Boston.
But his effectiveness nosedived late in the year, when he posted a 12.46 ERA and 2.538 WHIP over his final five appearances, walking six batters while striking out just four.
Those struggles clearly continued in Game 1, when Miller gave up a home run and an infield single in his one-third of an inning, but Tracy — with his full complement of high-leverage bullpen arms available — went right back to Miller in Game 2. For a second straight night, Miller could not deliver.
Tracy and the Red Sox felt comfortable giving the ball to Tolle in Game 1 on the road in Yankee Stadium. Yet with two outs and nobody on in the fifth, and with Tolle at just 83 pitches, Tracy took that ball away and gave it to a reliever in whom the manager should have lost trust.
Tracy and the Red Sox then felt comfortable giving the ball to Gray in Game 2, this time with the season hanging in the balance. Yet with two outs and two runners aboard in the fifth, Tracy again took the ball out of the hand of the trusted starter to place it in the shaky left hand of Miller.
Both times, the move did not work. And though the correlation may not be strictly scientific, both bullpen moves led to Game 1 and Game 2 spiraling out of control from that point forward.
Gray, who's set to become a free agent this offseason unless he retires, said that Tracy did not give him an explanation for the move. Gray was also asked if Boston would be a "destination" if he does choose to pitch again next year.
"I don't know," he answered.

NEW YORK — For the second year in a row, the Red Sox season ended where it began: at Yankee Stadium.
On Wednesday night, before September officially turned to October, marking the true beginning of the postseason, the Red Sox were sent packing, again, by the Yankees. Unlike last year in this round, there was no need for a third game. No need for Aaron Judge. No need for Giancarlo Stanton. The Red Sox lost 9-2 on Wednesday night, a day after getting blown out 9-0 in the opener.
Instead, only embarrassment lived. Only quietness existed inside a clubhouse that will have to chew on two humiliating losses in the American League Wild Card Series.
There will be plenty from this season worth pointing to.
The Red Sox were once 14 games under .500. Then came the midsummer streak when they rattled off 15 straight wins and went 27-3 from the start of July through the beginning of August. Willson Contreras's season was vital to this club's success. Caleb Durbin's toughness and grit helped set the tone. The offense showed some malleability, deviating from its pull-side approach and becoming less one-dimensional.
All of that happened. All of it mattered.
But don't let any of it obscure the reality. Don't let the front office twist this. Don't let it off the hook too easily. The front office pivoted to Durbin only once it missed out on Alex Bregman.
And when October arrived -- pardon, the end of September -- the Red Sox finished their season with one fewer postseason win than they had a year ago.
It has now been five years since postseason baseball was last played at Fenway Park, the longest October drought for the ballpark since 1976-85.
Don't be fooled by the summer surge. Don't be fooled by the progress.
This season wasn't a success.
"Uncompetitive." Isaiah Kiner-Falefa said afterward. "We got boat-raced. To lose in the Wild Card is unacceptable."
"I mean, right now it's, regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there were quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series," manager Chad Tracy said. "And that ended for us tonight."
'I would have liked to have been trusted'
Frustration mounted in the clubhouse afterward, too. For a second straight night, Tracy pulled his starter early for Erik Miller, and it immediately backfired.
This time, it was Sonny Gray, who had allowed just one run, a solo homer to Luis García Jr. in the top of the fourth. In the fifth, Gray worked around a Trent Grisham leadoff single, recording two outs on a force out and a groundout. Yet, after a Ben Rice single put runners at first and third, Tracy inexplicably ended Gray's evening at just 70 pitches with Cody Bellinger looming.
Instantly, much like Tuesday night, the Yankees capitalized. Bellinger laced a single to right, extending the lead to 2-0.
Forced to piece together the rest of the game with a bullpen that included appearances from Garrett Crochet and Garrett Whitlock, the Red Sox watched the Yankees pour on eight runs against their relievers.
A disgruntled Gray didn't hold back his sentiments following the outing.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League the third time through the order," Gray said. He then paused for a moment. "I think that's a fact. I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."
Gray was spot-on. He, indeed, was the best starter in the American League the third time through the order, carrying a 1.99 ERA in 45 ⅓ innings pitched, a large enough sample size.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that are telling you what to do, because this is baseball and the data is here to help us," Contreras said. "But at the end of the day, we're going to need experienced and veteran guys to win games."
That points to a larger issue that has followed lead executive Craig Breslow.
The April firing of manager Alex Cora and his staff might have been the right decision. Tracy (who was named the full-time skipper last week), ideally, is the manager that Breslow envisioned at the helm. But don't let their torrid summer misconstrue the split in the clubhouse. Some players remain convinced the new coaching staff had little to do with their success.
That might have been Gray's last time in a Red Sox uniform -- or in any uniform, as the 36-year-old has contemplated retirement. Asked if he would want to return next season to the Red Sox if he decided to play:
"I don't know," Gray responded.
Roster questions looming
Roman Anthony needs to prove he can stay healthy. He was pulled from Game 1 after re-aggravating the same right hand that kept him out for 101 games. Anthony went for an MRI in Boston early Wednesday morning before returning that afternoon. It's still unclear if he needs surgery.
"After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%, kind of as you would expect," he said. "But I think for me, it was to a point where it was tolerable, and I was taking certain swings that were sketchy but was still able to come back and recover enough to just be in there every single day. But ultimately, I just took a few swings here recently where that wasn't the case."
Remember the Big Three? Anthony, Kristian Campbell and Marcelo Mayer were supposed to represent the next wave of the Red Sox.
What do the Red Sox do with Campbell, who was stuck in Triple-A all season and put up subpar numbers? Mayer was supposed to be the heir apparent to Trevor Story. He was traded to San Francisco.
Surely, Story has aged out of being an everyday shortstop.
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela and right fielder Wilyer Abreu are proven everyday players. But if Anthony isn't healthy, the Red Sox will need to patch up left field. Jarren Duran might have played his last season in a Red Sox uniform, with many suspecting he will be traded in the offseason.
And, despite the offense coming alive this summer, that could be viewed as fool's gold. During their 37-game surge, the Sox hit .258 with a .445 slugging percentage and their run creation was 15% better than league average. Over their final 47 games, those numbers fell to a .236 average, .382 slugging percentage and they created runs 6% below the league-average mark.
Their late-season woes looked much more like the offense from the first 78 games, when the club hit .244 with a .385 slugging percentage, than the one that transformed its season.
"Obviously disappointed," Story said on getting bounced from the postseason. "A lot of thoughts, but proud of this group, proud of this team. With all the hate and everything going around, the way this team came together, we really turned the season around to get back into this position. It was something that was special."
The summer run was special, yes.
But don't let this club off the hook.
The season wasn't a success.

NEW YORK — Sonny Gray has been one of the top pitchers in the American League all season, and for much of Wednesday night he did everything he could to keep the Red Sox in the game.
But with two outs in the bottom of the fifth, with his team clinging to a 1-0 lead and runners at the corners after Yankees slugger Ben Rice tagged him for a single, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy decided to take the ball from his starter and go to Erik Miller to face Cody Bellinger, opting for a lefty-on-lefty matchup even though Gray was only at 70 pitches and Miller has been shaky to close the season.
The move didn’t work out. Bellinger hit an RBI single and the Yankees ultimately went on to score eight runs against the Red Sox bullpen, winning Game 2 by a lopsided score of 9-2 to complete the Wild Cad Series sweep.
Following the game Gray was candid about his displeasure with getting the hook.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that’s a fact. Yeah I would have liked to live or die with me in that moment but that’s the competitor I am,” Gray said. “I think you can probably ask the guys and they feel the same way. I felt strong, I felt confident, I felt convicted, but what can you do?”
“I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment,” Gray continued, adding later that he hasn’t spoken with Tracy yet and wasn’t sure if there would be any point.
Gray wasn’t the only Red Sox veteran miffed about the decision. Asked for his thoughts shortly afterwards, first baseman Willson Contreras responded only by zipping his lips.
Tracy explained that he decided to go to Miller because they had fallen behind and he felt he had to be aggressive, especially given how much the offense was struggling to score runs. The Yankees had already gotten a couple of hits against Gray in the inning, and with how reliable the bullpen has been throughout the season he decided to play the matchup in hopes of putting out the fire.
“We’re trailing. We’re struggling to score runs. And when you get in spots where struggling to score runs and you’re already trailing, you feel like you’ve got to be aggressive and go,” Tracy said.
“Our bullpen’s been great all year,” Tracy continued later. “It’s a case sometimes of depending on what the score is and how much wiggle room you have, if we were able to put up some runs and maybe have some more breathing room, we might be able to do that. But trying to be aggressive and create tough match-ups, and it just didn’t work out.”
Tracy also went to the bullpen early in Game 1 as well, pulling Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings in Boston’s eventual 9-0 loss. Tolle’s pitch count was a relatively modest 83 pitches at that point, and though the rookie took a much more charitable view than his older teammates, he admitted any starter would rather keep going in that spot.
“As a competitor as you want to go as long as you can. I think for me I see it as there’s people that are going to – I trust our bullpen and the way they’ve gone about this year, I think they’ve been incredible, they’ve picked me up more times than I can count,” Tolle said. “It’s the postseason, you’ve got to limit as much as you can so whenever those situations happen, for me, ok, this is what’s going to be best for the team.”

Willson Contreras Shades Red Sox's Use of Analytics in Video After Sonny Gray's Early Exit
Willson Contreras indicated he felt overuse of analytics led Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy to pull Sonny Gray from Wednesday's Wild Card round elimination loss after just 70 pitches against the New York Yankees.
Contreras initially responded to reporters asking about his reaction to Gray's fifth-inning exit from the 9-2 loss by miming zipping his lips before elaborating.
"It's not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers that are telling you what to do, because this is baseball," Contreras said (h/t SNY). "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you're going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
When asked if he felt the Red Sox relied too much on data, Contreras nodded as he said, "If you watch the game."
Tracy, who had also pulled Game 1 starter Payton Tolle early, called Gray off the mound with two runners on base, one out remaining and the Red Sox trailing by one run in the bottom of the fifth.
Gray was replaced by Erik Miller, who on his third pitch of the game allowed a two-RBI single from Cody Bellinger.
Tracy then turned to Garrett Crochet for the sixth inning. Crochet allowed a run and loaded the bases until he was removed for Garrett Whitlock, who allowed five more runs before he was able to close out the frame.
Tracy said after the elimination loss he used the same reasoning to pull Gray as he had to remove Tolle from a Game 1 shutout loss to the Yankees.
"We're trailing. We're struggling to score runs, and when you get into spots where you're struggling to score runs and you're already trailing, you feel like you've got to be aggressive," Tracy told reporters Wednesday night.
The Yankees will now advance to face the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS, while the Red Sox will concede their second Wild Card loss in as many years. Ranger Suárez, who was slated to start a potential deciding Game 3, will not pitch this postseason.
The Red Sox fired former manager Alex Cora and turned to Tracy following a 10-17 start to the season. Tracy lost his interim tag and inked a three-year extension after leading the club to clinch a postseason berth.
Tracy will now be tasked with helping his club find a way to respond next fall to scoring two runs across their two postseason games.

Willson Contreras provided one of the few good Red Sox swings in this embarrassing showing against the Yankees and then took another postgame whack at his team.
The first-year Red Sox slugger seemingly took aim at the organization’s analytics philosophy after their 9-2 Game 2 loss to the Yankees in a wild-card sweep.
“There’s a lot of things to get better at in each area of the game. If you watch the game, we have to get better at the game running, we have to get better at taking care of the stealers, we have to do a lot of different stuff,” said Contreras, who homered off Max Fried in the sixth inning. “It’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball.
“The data is here to help us but at the end of the day, you’re going to need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff that I would like to say, but I’ll state it like that.”
If there was any confusion about who Contreras, 34, was throwing under the bus, the line “you have computers telling you what to do” clears that all up.
The Red Sox, like any team that thrives in baseball, rely on analytics to help them.
There will always be a debate about how much of the human element should be blended into games versus specifically relying on data to make decisions.
Contreras received a follow-up question about whether the Red Sox rely too much on data, and provided a cryptic decision.
“If you watch the game,” he said, “if you watch the game.”
His shot at the “computers” is notable since it came after two seemingly analytics-driven decisions for the Red Sox backfired, one in each game.
First-year manager Chad Tracy pulled Payton Tolle in a 1-0 game to have lefty reliever Erik Miller face Ben Rice in the fifth inning in Game 1 and Rice promptly homered.
He tried a similar move Wednesday in yanking Sonny Gray in the fifth for Miller to face Cody Bellinger in a 1-0 game and the Yankees outfielder laced an RBI single.
When asked his thoughts on pulling Gray, Contreras did not verbally answer but said all he needed to say by instead pretending to sow his mouth shut.
Contreras also provided an interesting answer about what happened to the team’s once-scorching lineup, with Boston tearing the cover off the ball during its 32-5 run that saved its season and then slumping to end the regular season before this two-run showing over 18 postseason innings.
“That’s a good question,” he replied. I’m not going to answer it because I don’t want to give my honest answer. We got eliminated, that’s the bottom line.
Contreras is under contract with Boston for the 2027 season and the team holds a $17.5 team option for 2028, and he produced a career-best .901 OPS this past season.
Boston surely will aim this offseason to build a deeper lineup around him and Roman Antony and if the team value his two cents, it seems he’ll be telling them to forget the data and use their eyes.

Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Willson Contreras has never been one to hold back when speaking to the media, especially during his first year with the Red Sox.
As such, the veteran first baseman was candid when asked to summarize Boston’s brief two-game playoff series against the Yankees in the Wild Card round.
“We didn’t play good at all,” Contreras said. “We didn’t pitch. We didn’t hit. And when you don’t have those two, it’s tough to win. They played better than us. And that’s why they advanced.”
Boston was ultimately outscored, 18-2, and outhit, 26-7, in a lopsided playoff series against New York — with the Red Sox bats going cold for the second straight postseason.
Before Contreras clubbed a solo shot in the top of the sixth inning, the Red Sox had gone 26.2 innings without scoring a run in the playoffs — dating back to last year’s postseason series against New York.
Despite a 32-5 surge in July and August that revived Boston’s season, the Red Sox’ bats went quiet down the stretch — even before this two-game series. In September, Boston posted just a .219 batting average, including just a .163 batting average with runners in scoring position.
Speaking after Boston’s 9-2 season-ending loss on Wednesday, Contreras was evasive when asked what led to the Red Sox’ disheartening downturn after such a dominant stretch in July and August.
“That’s a good question,” Contreras said. “I’m not going to answer it because I don’t want to give my honest answer. But we got eliminated. That’s the bottom line. We didn’t produce. We didn’t execute any part of the game, and that’s why we [lost].
“I know that we had a really good stretch. I’m really proud of what we did in the past, like I said. We were able to turn the season around, for sure, 100 percent. But that’s not enough. It’s not enough. And at the end of the day, you win games in the regular season to clinch the playoff, but then falling short in the playoffs, it’s tough.”
While Boston’s dormant offense loomed large over this series, Contreras also seemed to take umbrage with Chad Tracy’s decision to pull Sonny Gray after just one earned run allowed and 70 total pitches on Wednesday.
After Gray was lifted after 4.2 innings of work, reliever Erik Miller immediately gave up an RBI single — giving New York a 2-0 lead at the time.
When asked about Gray’s quick hook, Contreras didn’t comment — instead signaling a “lips sealed” motion with his hands and mouth twice.
Whether it was inspired by the decision to remove Gray or other instances in which the Red Sox have leaned heavily on analytics or other tools in their baseball operations, Contreras stressed that teams can’t rely on those metrics to translate directly into results — especially in October.
“It’s not enough when you have talent, or you have data, or you have computers telling you what to do, because this is baseball,” Contreras said. “The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day, you need experience and veteran guys to win games. There’s a lot of stuff I would like to say, but I’ll state it like that.”
When asked if he feels there’s too much of a reliance on data and analytics in baseball today, Contreras replied: “If you watch the game. If you watch the game.”
Contreras — who set career highs in home runs (27) and RBI (81) in his first year with Boston — said that he’d be open to having conversations with chief baseball officer Craig Breslow about the team’s approach to data and analytics.
“At the end of the day, we can talk, we can share ideas, but like I said, I’m not making decisions,” Contreras said, per MassLive’s Christopher Smith. “And we’re not going to make decisions. We are employees. We get paid to play baseball and we get paid to be out there on the field to perform. I mean, that’s the bottom line. Of course, we can have some conversations.”
The Red Sox have plenty of work to do this offseason, whether that means bolstering their lineup and adding some pop to their batting order, clearing a logjam of underachieving players across the roster, or ideally getting several key cogs like Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet healthy.
Contreras, who suffered his fair share of bumps and bruises in 2026, said plenty needs to change if Boston wants to advance past the Wild Card round in 2027.
“At the end of the day, it’s not about data. It’s about executing the game plan,” he noted.

Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Red Sox Game 2 starter Sonny Gray did little to mask his disappointment on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium.
Both due to Boston’s 2026 season coming to a close after a 9-2 loss to New York — and the early hook from Red Sox manager Chad Tracy that pulled the veteran starter after just 70 pitches.
“I would have liked to be trusted in that moment,” Gray declared after Boston’s loss on Wednesday.
When Tracy emerged from the dugout to pull Gray from his start, the 36-year-old righty had limited New York to one run — a solo shot from Luis Garcia Jr. — over 4.2 innings, striking out five and giving up five hits.
“I felt good, I felt crisp, I felt sharp,” Gray noted. “I was executing what I wanted to do. I’m frustrated for sure. I’m not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions, but frustration was definitely one.”
But with New York running through its batting order for a third time, Tracy opted to pull his starter with runners on first and third and two outs.
For the second game in a row, Tracy turned to reliever Erik Miller as the next arm up.
In Game 1, Miller took over for Payton Tolle (4.2 innings, five hits, one earned run) and immediately gave up a solo shot to Ben Rice.
On Wednesday, Miller relinquished an RBI single to Cody Bellinger — with that run charged to Gray.
Postgame, Gray was candid about his limited workload and the decision to pull him before he faced the heart of New York’s order for the third time.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time,” Gray said. “I think that’s a fact. I would have liked [for Tracy] to live or die with me in that moment, but that’s the competitor I am.
“I think you can probably ask the guys and I think they felt the same way. So, I felt strong, I felt confident, I felt convicted. But what can you do, you know?”
For what it’s worth, Willson Contreras refused to comment — doing a “lips sealed” motion — when asked by reporters about his thoughts on Gray’s early hook.
As Brian Barrett of The Ringer noted, opposing hitters batted just .180 against Gray in their third plate appearance against him during his 2026 starts — ranking 6th out of 117 qualified starters.
But Tracy instead opted to roll with another reliever in Miller, noting postgame that he wanted to chase a matchup against Bellinger with runs at a premium.
Still, choosing a reliever who relies heavily on a slider like Miller was also a curious choice — considering that Bellinger batted .435 with three home runs in 23 at-bats against sliders delivered by lefties this season.
“We’re trailing, we’re struggling to score runs,” Tracy said. “And when you get in spots where you’re struggling to score runs and you’re already trailing, you feel like you’ve got to be aggressive and go. … Trying to be aggressive and create tough matchups. It just didn’t work out.”
It was a frustrating end for Gray, who remains uncertain about whether or not he’ll continue playing as he enters free agency this offseason. He was one of Boston’s top players this season — going 18-5 in the regular season with a 2.72 ERA.
“I don’t know what the future holds for me,” Gray noted. “I do know that I walked off that mound with my chest back and my chin up and I can definitely be proud that I left it all out there until the ball was taken out of my hands. I still left that mound with my chest up and my chin up and I can be proud of that.”
When asked if the Red Sox would still be a team he’d consider pitching for if he wants to continue playing, Gray replied: “I don’t know.”

Though Cody Bellinger didn't spend much of his childhood in the new Yankee Stadium, that should've been all the more motivation for him to join the Yankees and make this place sound like the old one as often as he possibly could. Payton Tolle getting the 83-pitch early hook in Game 1 was somewhat defensible. He was losing grip. He's past a career high in innings. They have the horses. Removing Sonny Gray from this do-or-die game before the end of the fifth inning, midway through a masterpiece, was one of the silliest bits of overmanaging you'll see. Bringing in Erik Miller, who was victimized with two outs in the fifth in Game 1 to get victimized again was even sillier.
Bellinger smoked a two-out RBI single off Miller to add a second run to the Yankees' lead. The next time he strode to the plate, he made a much larger impact.
Cody Bellinger cements Yankees' ownership of the Boston Red Sox
Gone. Very gone. In a snap, the Yankees turned two productive outs and a three-run mash into an 8-1 ballgame. Losing Garrett Whitlock, who surrendered the bomb, might've been the Yankees' most prudent Rule 5 Draft move in franchise history. It's called the long game.
For those keeping track at home, the 2026 Red Sox rode a 32-5 midsummer stretch to the postseason, reached within a half-game of the Yankees and got high on their own supply. From that point forward, they were much closer to .500, losing impact role players and stars alike by the bowlful. Sox fans were undeterred. They continued to crow. They loved to laugh at Aaron Judge's injury troubles. They purported to be inside Cam Schlittler's head. If they truly were in there, they might've been able to pick up some knowledge on what it takes for a pitcher to go deep into games in the postseason and dominate.
And so, for the second season in a row, the Yankees have flushed the Sox out of the postseason - Boston actually doesn't even reach October this year, which begins tomorrow. Last year, it was Schlittler, the Massachusetts native, growing up on the big stage. He helped this year, too.
But this time around, it ended with Tracy hooking Gray for no apparent reason and Bellinger, a son of pinstripes, delivering the crushing blow. Maybe, just maybe, order has returned to the universe and karma has begun to punish the brashness of Bostonians in new and unique ways. Whitlock gagging, Garrett Crochet disintegrating after an Adley Rutschman slow play (the trade target the Sox outbid the Yankees for, by the way), and Caleb Durbin making the final out ... in a game Gray should've owned ... was a pretty clever way to get it done.
Thanks, Belli.

NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston.
Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep.
Other WRAL Top Stories
“We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.
“The fans were electric from the first pitch and the boys were hungry. We got a young, hungry team here," Yankees captain Aaron Judge said as teammates sprayed him with bubbly during the clubhouse celebration. “This makes me feel young every single time.”
Judge missed this series because of a calf injury and isn't sure whether he will play against the Rays, who beat New York 7-6 in the season series.
“Saturday’s a long ways away," he said.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston's 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke open the game with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out leading off — with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBIs that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst that put New York ahead 8-1.
“Step one,” said Bellinger, who caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay, a 2000 Yankees World Series champion. “Now we got to go into Tampa and play against a tough team."
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, lost last year's wild-card matchup after defeating the Yankees in the opener.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there was quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series and that ended for us tonight, so it’s frustrating,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “There’s a lot of things you can say, but in the moment right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it’s going to take some time to get over that.”
Boston, which also got a seventh-inning homer from Nick Sogard off Will Warren, was missing leadoff hitter Roman Anthony because of a hand injury. The Red Sox were held to a .117 average in the series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and outscored 18-2.
New York hit .382 in the series. Boston's bullpen had a 20.25 ERA.
“We played great baseball in a lot of ways here, obviously anchored by our two great starters," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
Yankees batters hit .450 (9 for 20) with runners in scoring position after finishing 19th among the 30 teams with a .246 RISP during the regular season.
“I feel like it’s a whole new level from regular season to these last two days,” Austin Wells said.
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García's fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just relieved.
Gray was disappointed he wasn't allowed to face Bellinger.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that’s a fact,” Gray said. "I would’ve liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. And, yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. So I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted.”
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, throwing error, stolen base, bunt single and intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger's homer.
"I can’t believe they were willing to face a guy like Belli with men on base there," Rice said.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year's Wild Card Series opener, hadn't pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation when he bounced a sweeper off Adley Rutschman's chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled that Jones was out. The Yankees appealed and the call was reversed by the video umpire at the commissioner's office.
“I couldn’t believe he was there,” Boone said. "I saw the ball squirt away a little bit. I didn’t think that much of it, and looked up and I was, like, 'Oh, he’s safe.'''
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Wells' sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout and Rice, who had four hits and six RBIs in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats.
Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“Definitely wasn’t sharp from the get-go but just wanted to challenge them, not try to give any free passes, especially in the first inning," Fried said.
After a night of celebration and a day off, the Yankees will head to Florida on Friday.
“There’s just so much more to do,” Bellinger said after the big night with his father on hand. “So obviously enjoy the moment, understand how cool it is, but keep on going.”
Up Next
New York RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.

item.content:encoded:
Heading into the Wild Card Series, one could make a case that the Red Sox had a chance to beat the Yankees. It would take two or three great starts from Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and/or Ranger Suarez, it would take some timely hitting to put two or three runs on the board per game, and it would take some lockdown relief innings from the back end of the bullpen.
Yet the Red Sox only got decent starts from Tolle and Gray, they set a new franchise record for offensive utility, and their bullpen was a catastrophe.
And the cherry on top was that their manager, who inked a contract extension last week, showed he certainly does not know how to manage in the postseason.
Other than that, did you enjoy the series?
Here's everything we learned from the ever-so-brief two-game sweep in the Wild Card Series, as the 2026 team technically failed to get as far as the 2025 Red Sox.
Red Sox set ugly new franchise record
Red Sox history spans 126 seasons, so it was a bit surprising to see the broadcast note early in Game 2 that Boston was in the midst of rewriting franchise history with the longest scoring drought to start a postseason ever.
Obviously, the Red Sox' offense has been stagnant (or worse) for weeks, but 26 previous trips to the playoffs, you'd figure that they had started off with a scoreless game and a half before.
Alas, nope. This drought was historic. It ended at 14.2 innings, broken by Willson Contreras' solo shot with two outs in the sixth inning.
And while some of it may be explained by the absences of Roman Anthony and Mickey Gasper, there's no excuse for a playoff team to be this helpless at the plate.
Chad Tracy is not a big-game manager right now
There may have been a case for Chad Tracy to pull Payton Tolle for Erik Miller in Game 1. Not really, but there could have been a case made for Miller's sinker being more effective against Ben Rice than Tolle's fastball.
Yet there's simply no way to understand why one night later, Tracy made the exact same move.
With Sonny Gray at just 70 pitches and the Yankees leading 1-0 with two outs in the fifth inning, Tracy went back to Miller, this time with two runners on base and Cody Bellinger at the plate. The left-left matchup was presumably the reason for the call, but Bellinger crushes sliders from lefties. And when Miller threw a slider to Bellinger ... he delivered.
Bellinger singled home a run, and Miller then gave up another hit to Luis Garcia Jr. The Red Sox only got out of the inning because Rice was caught at home after an aggressive send on that second single.
Gray's pitch count of 70 was tied for his second-lowest of the season, and though he had allowed two singles in the fifth, his body of work over the season and over the past 13 years gave him a much better chance of escaping the mini jam than Miller, who had a 2.045 WHIP and 7.36 ERA in the month of September and who gave up a home run and a single while getting just one out the night before.
If Tracy was insistent that Gray had to come out of the game, he had, quite literally, every high-leverage arm available to him. Instead, he went with Erik Miller.
And with that same complement of arms available in the bottom of the sixth inning, Tracy went with Garrett Crochet, who hasn't pitched in a game since April 25. It didn't go well.
Tracy also showed a lack of feel for the moment when he let leadoff hitter Jahmai Jones, who batted .129 with a .432 OPS over the final 13 games of the regular season and who struck out looking twice, to take his third at-bat in the sixth inning, with the Red Sox trailing 2-0.
Given Boston's offensive ineptitude, the bullpen decisions are perhaps all moot. But had this been a close series, or if the Red Sox find themselves in one in the future, Tracy will carry some major doubt regarding his ability to manage those games.
Simply put, Chad Tracy did not do a single thing right in these two high-stakes games.
More Red Sox Coverage
Luis Garcia Jr.'s home run was great hitting, not bad pitching
It took until the fourth inning for the Yankees to get to Sonny Gray, but the solo homer he allowed to Luis Garcia Jr. didn't come on a bad pitch at all.
Leading off the fourth, Garcia was behind in the count 1-2 when Gray tried to bury a sweeper down and in to the lefty. Gray hit his spot with a pitch that was set to hit the bottom of the strike zone. But Garcia simply stayed on the pitch and went down and got it.
Luis Gar-SEE-YA 🦁 pic.twitter.com/GqxScAqskG
— New York Yankees (@Yankees) October 1, 2026
With the Red Sox starved for runs, Garcia's solo shot was a jarring reminder that all it takes is one good swing to put a run on the board.
Boston eventually got that swing from Contreras in the sixth, but that jolt of hope for the visiting team didn't last long.
What could have been with Garrett Crochet ...
If you just looked at the box score, you'd be shocked to see Garrett Crochet's line. He faced four batters, allowing all of them to score. He didn't record an out, despite getting Spencer Jones to chase strike three to start the sixth inning.
Of course, some of that outcome was fair, as Crochet allowed back-to-back singles. But Caleb Durbin couldn't get the out at first on what was intended to be a sacrifice bunt, Crochet left with the bases loaded, and Garrett Whitlock -- who had a dreadful night -- couldn't limit the damage at all.
Such an outcome was perhaps expected, considering Crochet has not pitched in a game since April 25 due to shoulder problems. But you also can't help but wonder what would have happened if Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras hadn't combined to bungle Crochet's inning-opening strikeout of Jones.
Rutschman took an extra beat to pounce on the ball that had bounced off his chest, and then he took an extra step before firing to first base. There, Contreras was planted on the back side of the base instead of the front. As a result, Jones was able to beat the throw.
Credit to Aaron Boone for challenging that call, which was initially an out on the field, but really, it wasn't even close.
Rutschman then compounded the matter by sailing a throw into center field when Jones stole second, allowing the runner to take third before scoring on a single. Had Rutschman made either of those two throws, it's fair to wonder how differently Crochet's inning could have gone.
Summing up the season
There will be plenty of time in the coming months to eulogize this season, but really, despite the 32-5 stretch in the summer, it wasn't one to celebrate.
Last year's team won a game in the Wild Card Series, a disappointing ending. This year's team couldn't even do that.
Injuries to Crochet and Anthony were certainly impactful, but this roster -- and particularly the offense -- was not built to contend for a World Series. The Red Sox scored two or fewer runs in 13 of their final 23 games, averaging 2.5 runs per game over that stretch.
With the season on the line, the Red Sox had Jahmai Jones, Nate Eaton and Nick Sogard in their starting lineup.
After trading three of their top-five prospects to acquire Adley Rutschman, the catcher batted .222 with a .688 OPS in the regular season before going 1-for-8 in the playoffs.
Willson Contreras, a 34-year-old former catcher with a lot of MLB miles on him, was worn down by the end of the season. Caleb Durbin, whose lows outnumbered his highs this year, went 0-for-7 in the playoffs. Ceddanne Rafaela posted the same numbers, too.
The return for Marcelo Mayer was Erik Miller, who made a strong first impression but played a pivotal role in sinking the team's chances in both postseason losses after an extremely unreliable final month of the season.
The starting pitching staff was excellent, and the bullpen was elite. But the overall roster construction will lead to plenty of questions about Craig Breslow's ability to build a real winner. Likewise, the two playoff games cast some serious doubt on whether Chad Tracy is a manager capable of winning games in October.
The 15-game winning streak and 32-5 stretch might have led to some internal victory laps and the decisions to stick with Breslow and Tracy for the foreseeable future. But the 2026 Red Sox, on the whole, were what they were: mediocre. And having been stuck in mediocrity (or worse) for half a decade, there won't be much more patience in and around Boston for it to continue.
Technically, the historic season turnaround may have been a positive, as making the playoffs beats bottoming out more often than not. But considering that the Red Sox likely could have loaded up on promising players by selling off veteran pieces like Contreras, Gray, Aroldis Chapman and anyone else at the deadline, that run in July may have hurt the Red Sox in the long term -- especially with the prospect haul that went out to acquire Rutschman.
In any event, the Red Sox finished as the third-best team in the AL East, and they failed to win a single playoff game, getting outscored 18-2 in their lone playoff series. That's the final word on the season as the long offseason -- potentially longer than most -- awaits.

Boston Red Sox fans didn't want to see Chad Tracy emerge from the dugout in the bottom of the fifth inning. He should've learned from his Game 1 mistake.
But in Wild Card Game 2, Tracy pulled Sonny Gray after 4.2 frames to swap him for Erik Miller, just as he did with Payton Tolle the day before. Gray was having a better night than Tolle, though — he collected five strikeouts and allowed two runs on six hits. He was living on the edges and racked up swing-and-miss through 70 pitches.
Miller entered the game and immediately let up a single to Cody Bellinger. The Yankees took a 2-0 lead. The run was charged to Gray, but it didn't have to be that way. Miller posted a brutal September and struggled similarly in his first Wild Card outing. The choice to turn to him again, especially with the season on the line, is inexplicable.
Tracy's bullpen management didn't get any better. Garrett Crochet entered the game in the sixth inning and immediately got unlucky. Spencer Jones struck out swinging at a pitch in the dirt and Adley Rutschman couldn't get a good block on it, which allowed Jones to take first base. Crochet pitched decently well, avoiding the middle of the plate, but he couldn't collect an out before New York plated another run and loaded the bases.
Chad Tracy pulling Sonny Gray early led to the Red Sox's downfall in Wild Card Game 2, as it did in Game 1 with Payton Tolle
Going to Crochet while the game was still within reach was another strange choice by Tracy. Crochet hadn't pitched in the big leagues since April 25 due to two different shoulder injuries — the Red Sox had no idea how he would fare in a game, but went to him anyway despite having Jake Bennett available.
Tracy's bullpen management choices certainly didn't make the Red Sox any better this series, but their offense deserves some blame for the way the Wild Card series went. Willson Contreras and Nick Sogard contributed solo home runs to prevent another shutout, but no one else gave them any help. Four hits, seven strikeouts and 0-for-2 with runners in scoring position won't cut it against any playoff team, let alone the Yankees' utterly dominant pitching staff.
Even so, Boston got more offense in the win-or-go-home game than it did in Game 1, and bad bullpen management did the Red Sox in again. Had Tracy kept Gray in the game, the score could've stayed closer and the game might've actually been winnable. Instead, an incredible, memorable season came to an end without ever reaching October, and the Red Sox did it to themselves.
