NEW YORK (AP) — With the Boston bats ice cold at Yankee Stadium again, a couple of quick hooks by Red Sox rookie manager Chad Tracy led to another early postseason exit.
And top starter Sonny Gray wasn't happy about being lifted after only 70 pitches.
"I think I'm the best pitcher in the American League going through the order the third time. I think that's a fact," Gray said. "I would have liked to have been trusted in that moment."
For the second consecutive season, the Red Sox were sent home for the winter by their biggest rivals as the New York Yankees rolled to a 9-2 victory Wednesday night and a two-game sweep of their Wild Card Series.
Boston was outscored 18-2 overall and left to lament a miserable finish to this roller-coaster ride of a season that included Tracy taking over when Alex Cora was fired in April.
Tracy's decision-making came under scrutiny after both playoff games against the Yankees. In Boston's 9-0 defeat a night earlier, Tracy pulled rookie starter Payton Tolle after 4 2/3 innings and 83 pitches in a 1-0 game.
Last year, the Red Sox won their Wild Card Series opener before losing to New York in a deciding Game 3 as they got overpowered by Cam Schlittler, who pitched another playoff gem against his hometown team Tuesday night.
"To have it end here two times in a row is tough," shortstop Trevor Story said.
Facing a Yankees lineup missing injured slugger Aaron Judge, the Red Sox gave up 26 hits in two games despite a pair of effective performances from their starting pitchers.
At the plate, Boston mustered only seven hits and finally snapped a 26-inning postseason scoring drought that dated to last year when Willson Contreras homered just over the right-center fence in the sixth Wednesday.
"It's obviously been an eventful year," Tracy said. "In the moment right now you can't think much more other than anything but the fact that we just lost a playoff series."
Needing a victory to extend their season, the Red Sox sent Gray to the mound and the 18-game winner certainly gave them a chance. Boston trailed 1-0 in the fifth when the right-hander allowed a two-out single to Ben Rice that put runners at the corners.
Tracy then yanked Gray, eager to hand the ball to baseball's best bullpen during the regular season.
"I felt good. You know, I felt crisp. I felt sharp. I felt like I was just out there competing. And yeah, I mean, I got clipped for a solo homer and then some singles, but I felt like I stayed on the attack throughout. I was just executing what I wanted to do," Gray said. "I'm frustrated, for sure. You know, not ready for it to end. A lot of emotions."
Asked about the move, Contreras put his finger over his lips to zip them shut.
"It's not enough when you have talent or you have data or you have computers that's telling you what to do, because this is baseball," he said. "The data is here to help us, but at the end of the day you are going to have to need experience and veteran guys to win games."
In both games of the series, Tracy gave the ball to left-handed reliever Erik Miller after taking out his starting pitcher.
On Tuesday, Rice greeted Miller with a 423-foot solo homer to straightaway center field.
On Wednesday, Tracy summoned Miller to face a different left-handed hitter, Cody Bellinger — who batted .274 against lefties this season and .259 versus right-handers. In fact, his .310 batting average against left-handers over the past two years was the best of any left-handed hitter in the majors.
Bellinger made Tracy and the Red Sox pay, lining an RBI single to right field.
"We're struggling to score runs," Tracy said. "And when you get in spots where you're struggling to score runs and you're already trailing, you feel like you've got to be aggressive and go."
Back from a shoulder injury, ace starter Garrett Crochet entered in the sixth for his first outing since April 25 and first relief appearance since 2023 with the Chicago White Sox. The left-hander opened with a strikeout, but Spencer Jones reached safely on a wild pitch, and Crochet never got an out.
Bellinger's three-run homer off right-hander Garrett Whitlock capped a six-run inning that made it 8-1, and the Red Sox were done. A bullpen that led the majors with a 3.00 ERA during the regular season finished this series with a 20.25 ERA after giving up 15 runs, 15 hits and seven walks in 6 2/3 innings, with a .484 opponents' batting average.
Boston's latest downfall in the Bronx was a crushing end to a wild 2026 season for the Red Sox, who stumbled to a 32-46 start. Tracy was the skipper at Triple-A Worcester before getting promoted to interim manager in Boston, and the team finally began to take off with a four-game sweep of the Yankees at Fenway Park in late June.
After clinching a wild-card spot last week, the Red Sox removed the interim tag and named Tracy the 49th manager in team history, signing him to a three-year contract that runs through the 2029 season, with a club option for 2030. The team also exercised the 2029 and 2030 options on chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.
"I wasn't there for the highs and lows," Crochet said. "For this team to do what it did do, to make it to this point, was nothing short of miraculous."
Led by Gray and Contreras, among others, the Red Sox went on a 15-game winning streak in July that equaled a franchise record and used a 32-5 surge to climb back into contention. They became the fourth team in major league history to reach the postseason after falling 14 games under .500, and the first to qualify after losing as many as 44 of its first 75.
Gray, who can become a free agent after the World Series, went around the clubhouse to hug each of his teammates following Wednesday's defeat.
"I'm proud of what we accomplished," the pitcher said. "We were left for dead there for a while."

Roman Anthony out of Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of Wild Card Series
The Red Sox season will rest on the arm of starting pitcher Sonny Gray as the team takes on the New York Yankees on Wednesday in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series.
The Sox won't have the services of Roman Anthony, who appeared to reaggravate his hand injury during the team's 9-0 loss in Game 1.
"We actually sent him back to Boston last evening to get there so he could be early in the morning and re-image the hand, which shows additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren't there before," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. "So he's sore and obviously not in the lineup."
Anthony will be replaced on the roster by infielder Curtis Mead, who broke his wrist during his debut with the Red Sox on July 27. Anthony would eligible to return to the lineup for the American League Championship Series.
The Sox will have long odds to beat to continue their playoff run. Teams taking a 1-0 lead in a three-game wild-card series have gone on to win that series 21 out of 24 times, 17 times with a sweep.
Home teams have won all nine series in which they have won the first game.
On Tuesday, Yankees starter Cam Schlittler and the rest of the pitching staff held the Sox to just three hits.
Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle might have been the team's best player, but manager Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning of a 1-run game. Reliever Erik Miller immediately gave up a homer to Dartmouth College graduate Ben Rice, and it was all downhill from there.
On Wednesday night, Gray will pitch opposite Yankees starter Max Fried.

The Red Sox are up against the wall. Cam Schlittler, once again, shoved against the Red Sox in game one, throwing 117 pitches in a 6.1-inning shutout before handing it over to the bullpen. Paul Blackburn and John Schreiber shut the door, keeping the Red Sox off the scoreboard to win game one, 9-0. Coming into this season, the winner of game one has won 15 of 16 Wild Card series since playoff expansion. The only exception is the Yankees over the Red Sox last season.
If the Red Sox want to keep their season alive, it comes down to Sonny Gray. Let's think about it in innings. The Red Sox used five relievers on Tuesday night: Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Alec Gamboa, Wyatt Olds, and Brayan Bello.
Erik Miller was excellent immediately after being acquired, but his September, as well as his career-long control issues, should reduce him to only low-leverage spots. Greg Weissert can potentially provide an inning, but he's not an arm to trust on back-to-back days in a sticky spot. Alec Gamboa and Wyatt Olds were both late additions to the roster, and neither looked particularly up to the job in game one, while Brayan Bello has never pitched two days in a row in the major leagues.
That leaves Ranger Suarez, Garrett Crochet, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman, and Jake Bennett as the unused pitchers, alongside today's starter Sonny Gray.
Ranger Suarez is set to start game three. Garrett Crochet is a complete unknown. He hasn't pitched since April, and he was ineffective when he was on the mound. If he's healthy, I'd expect him to be able to get outs, but who knows where he's truly at health-wise. Garrett Whitlock has been one of the best relievers in baseball, but his longest outing of the season is 1.1 innings. He's only thrown more than 30 pitches once this season, and it came in an outing in which he walked two hitters. Extending him for more than one inning could be a tricky proposition. And then there's Aroldis Chapman. Chapman, like Whitlock, has been fantastic, but hasn't got more than three outs in a game this season. If you put those three arms together and assign two innings to Crochet, that's four innings. Of course, given the stakes, they could extend Whitlock or Chapman, but their effectiveness after three outs is a relative mystery. If you want to give Jake Bennett an inning or two, you could, but he doesn't seem like an arm they'd go to unless they were trailing, and there's no need to eat innings in a do-or-die game.
The offense was, at least in terms of scoring, the worst in baseball in September. Roman Anthony was lost in the middle of game one, and the rest of the lineup couldn't touch Schlittler. If I were a betting man, I wouldn't put money on them putting a lot of runs on the board against Max Fried. If they want a chance to win the game, they'll need to keep the Yankees off the board, and with the lack of quality innings in the bullpen, that means getting length out of Sonny Gray.
Gray has been the Red Sox best starter by ERA this season. He's gone at least six innings in 22 of his 29 starts. In two starts against the Yankees, he's allowed three earned runs over 13.2 innings pitched with 12 strikeouts and 3 walks. Despite a 14-year career, Gray has only thrown in six postseason games. In those six games, he has a 3.26 ERA, but has only pitched more than five innings once (an 8-inning shoutout for the Athletics against the Tigers in 2013). For the Red Sox to win today, they need Sonny Gray to turn in one of the best postseason performances of his career.
Fortunately, Chad Tracy can unload the clip in game two, because in playoff baseball terms, game three might as well be in six months. The Red Sox need to play every card they have to keep the season alive, but Sonny Gray keeping the Yankees off the scoreboard for as long as possible is the key.

Payton Tolle had just retired Paul Goldschmidt for the third time on one pitch, running his pitch count to a manageable 83 with two outs in the fifth inning Tuesday, when Chad Tracy decided he’d seen enough.
With Boston trailing by one run and Ben Rice, who doubled in the first inning, due up next, the manager opted to remove his pitcher who had settled into the pitching duel by that point.
And it backfired in horrible fashion for Boston.
Lefty reliever Erik Miller immediately surrendered a long solo homer to center field to Rice — the first of his two against Boston relievers — and it completely changed the tone of the game in Boston’s 9-0 loss to the Yankees in Game 1 of the AL Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium.
Boston’s b-tier relievers ultimately surrendered eight runs in 3 1/3 innings.
“Not just the pitch count necessarily, but you’re trailing already, you’re moving through the third time,” Tracy said. “Rice had already hit a double in the gap off of him, and you have a nice lane there for Miller, and obviously he got him. Just felt like it was the time to go.”
This postseason marks Tracy’s first calling the shots and moments like this one Tuesday night are what ultimately can swing series.
Sure, Boston did not score, but being down 1-0 to Cam Schlittler and the Yankees bullpen is a vastly different world than trailing by two entering the seventh.
Tolle allowed four hits over the first nine batters but settled down to retire eight of the next 10 batters and navigated a two-on, no-outs situation in the fifth while trailing 1-0.
He began the sixth by retiring Austin Wells on six pitches and then sitting down Goldschmidt, leaving him certainly with room to possibly navigate six innings if he worked effectively.
Tracy, though, opted for a new look in Miller, ending Tolle’s day after 4 2/3 innings of one-run ball.
“I thought he threw the ball well,” Tracy said. “They did an effective job of grinding the count up as well. He had traffic. They put traffic on him. He was able to navigate his way through that. I think he competed extremely well for the time that he was out there and gave us what he could.
“I think the number being up there in the mid-80s, still trying to get through five, probably higher than what you normally see with Payton, and to be expected in an environment like this. But I thought he competed his butt off.”
Miller, a midseason trade acquisition, struggled to end the regular season and those issues carried over to the postseason when he fired a middle-middle 97-mph heater that Rice hit out to dead center.
Tolle said that as a competitor, he felt he could have gone longer but understood the decision due to the strength of Boston’s bullpen during the regular seaosn.
Boston is now one loss away from a second straight early postseason exit at the Yankees’ hands.
“Wasn’t good enough,” Tolle said. “They had a good plan and I threw a lot of balls … just didn’t feel like I could command the zone, kind of let some at-bats get away from me. A lot of pitches.”
He added about the bullpen: “Those guys picked me up a lot this year.”

Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman, and Caleb Durbin will join the lineup in hopes to scrape together more than the six total runs they scored last season. Crochet could end up joining the bullpen in his return from injury, along with newcomers Erik Miller and Jake Bennett, which is a pretty decent group of pitchers being added to one of the very best units in baseball this season.
The Yankees will also be in a better position on the pitching side, with Gerrit Cole serving as the do-or-die option behind Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Luis Garcia Jr., Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. should help the lineup against left-handers, though there is something to be said about the so-so status of Aaron Judge.
If we can boil all of that down, though, only one man can completely swing the series…
Chad Tracy.
Tracy’s most difficult decisions might come before the season even starts, as he will be relied upon heavily to figure out who will fill out the roster — Braiden Ward? Jarren Duran? Curtis Mead? Jahmai Jones? Nate Eaton? Isiah Kiner-Falefa? Crochet?
It’s not going to be easy, but all of that pales in comparison to making decisions with who will play, when they will play, and how he manages things when the lights are at their brightest in The Bronx.
“It’s the playoffs, so we’re at the point in the season where teams that are remaining need to win or they’re going home,” Tracy said during his media availability on Monday. “I have a feel for that.
“… It’s all hands on deck. I think everyone is aware that during the playoffs it’s about winning moments and being aggressive — all those things. I think most of our guys who have been around understand that, so we’re going to go out and play our butts off and manage and do everything we can to win each game.”
Alex Cora, the manager of last year’s squad that became the first in history to lose the best-of-three series after taking a lead, made some… interesting decisions in hindsight.
Bello was pulled after 2 1/3 innings in Game 2, which led to Justin Wilson, Zack Kelly, Garrett Whitlock, and Tolle being used out of the bullpen and becoming unavailable for Game 3. Nate Eaton started over Wilyer Abreu in Game 2. Rob Refsnyder got two starts over Masataka Yoshida, which makes sense considering they faced two left-handers, but he finished 0-for-5 while the latter went 4-for-7. Nathaniel Lowe played in all three games, while Nick Sogard only played in two.
It’s easy to go back in time and poke holes though these decisions with the benefit of hindsight, but that’s kind of the whole point in looking ahead at the same two teams playing each other again with one of them being led by someone new.
Tracy needs to avoid making similar mistakes, and he needs to do it without the benefit of years of experience in similar situations. The Red Sox stripped him of that interim tag because they believe he can, and it’s only a matter of time before we find out whether or not they’re right.

A whopping 503 days. That was the time frame between Tanner Houck’s last start in the major leagues and his start in game 162 of this season. The right-hander missed significant time after an attempted rehab assignment in 2025 ultimately led to Tommy John surgery back in August of 2025.
Despite the timeline for Tommy John surgery typically taking close to a full season before a pitcher can begin throwing seriously in a rehab assignment, Houck had a plan in place for being back on a mound and throwing meaningful innings by the end of September of this season. To get there, he worked extremely hard, getting into rehab assignments with Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester before their respective seasons concluded.
And after just over 12 months of rehab and recovery, Houck kept to his word. The right-hander was given the start for the Boston Red Sox's final game before the playoffs and showed flashes of his past dominance. Tossing three innings, Houck took the loss as he allowed three runs (all of them on two Alex Bregman home runs) on four hits while not walking a batter and getting one strikeout. In the outing, he tossed exactly 50 pitches, roughly what he threw during his rehab appearances.
Despite the positive stat line for a pitcher making his first start in over a year and a half, there were some concerns for Houck, namely that his velocity was down from even 2025, a sign that the right-hander is still working on ramping back up. His sinker, which he threw 15 times yesterday, averaged just 92.4 mph compared to its 94.5 mph from the 2025 season. Even his four-seam fastball saw a decline of almost two mph as it averaged 93.3 mph compared to 95 mph in 2025. The right-hander also struggled to miss bats, getting just one whiff out of 24 swings by the Chicago Cubs.
Despite that, he still showcased some positives that could help his chance of being on the playoff roster. Despite giving up a home run early in the game to Bregman, Houck didn’t fall apart. Instead, the right-hander followed that up by retiring seven of the next eight batters he faced, giving the offense a chance to get back into the game. That string of retired batters was then broken up with one out in the third inning as Bregman took a sweeper that caught too much of the plate and deposited it into left field to put the Cubs back ahead 3-2. Houck then finished his outing by getting the next two batters out before giving way to the bullpen for the fourth inning.
Despite taking the loss in what would eventually be a 6-2 Cubs win, Houck was around where he should be in his return from injury. Not completely dominant, but good enough to give the team a chance to win with his outing. Outside of his two mistakes to Bregman, Houck only allowed two hits, both of them singles. In a relief role, that would be a welcomed performance if he can limit the long balls, especially with the Red Sox having lost Tyron Guerrero right before the playoffs.
While it might not seem likely for Houck to make the playoff roster, the sudden loss of Guerrero opens a path for the right-hander. While his velocity is nothing in comparison to the flamethrower, Houck has experience out of the bullpen as he served as closer briefly in 2022, earning eight saves before an injury ended his season. That’s not even talking about how in the 2021 playoffs he came out of the bullpen five times. Despite the struggles he had that season, the experience would be appreciated for a bullpen that, outside of Aroldis Chapman and Garrett Whitlock, has very minimal playoff experience.
He may not look like a high-leverage reliever at the moment, but he could help shorten the game and bridge the gap to the back-end of the bullpen. As a bulk reliever, he could be relied upon to take the ball from one of the starting pitchers and hand it to an arm like Whitlock or even Erik Miller who will be asked to step up with the loss of Guerrero. In his lone outing this year, Houck surrendered six hard hit balls, though two of them were the home runs he surrendered. Of the remaining four, only one (the first hit he allowed all game) turned into a hit. With the defense Boston has lined up behind him, Houck could be able to allow a hard hit ball here or there and still mitigate the damage.
The biggest concern, however, is the velocity, which will limit his ability to get swings and misses. Everyone knows the age-old thought that velocity plays in the postseason—just look back at the 2018 Red Sox roster that had a bullpen containing Joe Kelly, Matt Barnes and Heath Hembree. With Houck being in the low to mid-90s at the moment, the team could decide to turn their attention to a harder thrower.
Whatever decision the Red Sox make with Houck, it’s a positive sign that he stepped back onto a major-league mound as quickly as he did. His future is a lot less murky with his return officially in the books.

After a long rollercoaster of a season, the Chicago Cubs and Boston Red Sox will close it out at Tropicana Field due to a dangerous nor'easter over Massachusetts and many other states. The Red Sox and Cubs have both clinched playoff spots so the outcome of game 162 can't benefit or hinder either team.
Because of the lack of stakes, the Red Sox can take a risk. Tanner Houck will start the game for Boston after spending the entire season on the injured list healing Tommy John surgery, according to Tim Healey of The Boston Globe.
There has been no report on the expected length of Houck's start. The Red Sox could try to get multiple innings out of him to rest as many pitchers as possible, or he could pitch one or two frames with a bullpen game to follow. Jen McCaffrey of The Athletic reports that Houck has been built up for about three innings of work, but an appearance of that length could take him out of consideration for Red Sox's Wild Card roster since he's fresh off a long-term injury (subscription required).
Houck hasn't pitched in the big leagues since May 12, 2025. After he posted a career-best 3.12 ERA as Boston's ace in 2024, Houck experienced a severe regression in 2025. He logged an 8.04 ERA and 1.69 WHIP over 43.2 frames last season. The Red Sox optioned him to Triple-A to figure out his struggles, but he never looked as good as he did the year before. Late in the season, Boston discovered his injury and he underwent surgery.
Red Sox activate Tanner Houck for surprise game 162 start, put Tyron Guerrero back on IL with shoulder issue
Houck and the Red Sox have been pushing for the righty's return as a bullpen arm, and there's now an easy roster spot for him after more brutal Sox injury news. Tyron Guerrero has been placed back on the injured list with a shoulder strain. Healey reports that the injury will keep him out for at least the first two rounds of the postseason.
Guerrero was on the IL from September 1-20 with right shoulder inflammation and losing him again is a crushing blow for Boston's bullpen. The flamethrower quickly emerged as a key setup man for the Sox this year and they'll be short a dangerous option in the later innings. He posted a 3.10 ERA, 1.11 WHIP, 41 strikeouts and eight walks over 40.2 frames this season.
Guerrero's absence puts more pressure on the Sox's relief arms to maintain the high standard they've set as a group this year (league-best 2.99 ERA). Houck will hopefully be joined in the bullpen by Garrett Crochet, who is also hopinig to make a triumphant return as a reliever in the coming days. Boston will also need lefty setup man Erik Miller at his best following some recent mechanical struggles.

Guardians eke out 1-0 win over Red Sox, clinch playoff berth
(Photo credit: Paul Rutherford)
Angel Martinez's second-inning home run was all the visiting Guardians needed for a 1-0 win over the Boston Red Sox on Thursday night, allowing Cleveland to clinch its third consecutive American League playoff berth.
While Martinez provided the only offense, Joey Cantillo (11-9) dominated for five shutout innings behind opener Daniel Espino. Cantillo allowed just one hit and two walks and striking out four. He has not allowed a run across his last three outings (15 innings) as a bulk reliever.
The Guardians (83-76) totaled four hits but allowed only two to the Red Sox (85-74) en route to winning the decisive game of the three-game series. Boston earned a 1-0 victory on Wednesday.
Cleveland logged its seventh win in eight games to remain one game ahead of the Chicago White Sox (82-77) atop the AL Central. Both teams have three regular-season games remaining.
The playoff-bound Red Sox fell for the fourth time in five games despite getting five innings of one-run ball from Ranger Suarez (8-5). He struck out five and allowed three hits and one walk.
Espino bookended his 1-2-3 first inning with strikeouts.
The lone run came in the second, as Martinez broke up Suarez's four-up, four-down start with a 319-foot solo homer inside Pesky's Pole in right field.
Suarez escaped a two-on jam in the third with back-to-back outs and retired the final eight Guardians he faced.
Both bullpens were very strong. Hunter Gaddis allowed the sole hit in relief of Cantillo, a Jarren Duran single in the seventh, but they came after a leadoff walk in the frame was erased in a 6-4-3 double play.
Cleveland's Erik Sabrowski struck out two in the eighth, and Cade Smith fanned the side in a 1-2-3 ninth for his 41st save of the season.
Boston's Patrick Sandoval, Erik Miller and Raymond Burgos allowed just one combined hit across four shutout innings after Suarez departed. Burgos pitched hitless ball over the final two frames.
--Field Level Media

In these waning days of the regular season, the Red Sox are trying something new: Patrick Sandoval, reliever.
Sandoval tossed a scoreless sixth inning in a 1-0 loss to the Guardians on Thursday, his first appearance out of the bullpen since 2021.
It was a successfully uneventful frame at Fenway Park: After José Ramírez grounded a single through the left side of the infield and stole second, Sandoval retired Chase DeLauter (strikeout looking), Jo Adell (ground out), and Angel Martínez (ground out). His velocity was down a tad in the small sample size of 12 pitches (10 strikes), but he was pitching just three days after his most recent start.
Ahead of the playoffs opening Tuesday, the Sandoval twist is of particular note because of his recent struggles as a starter and the Red Sox’ recent struggles looking for a reliable lefthanded reliever.
As a member of the rotation, Sandoval had a 5.15 ERA in 13 outings this year. That included a 7.32 mark in four starts this month. He has appeared unlikely to fit into the postseason plans in that role.
Also of late, Erik Miller, the team’s top lefty reliever, has had a bad time, entering the day with a 8.53 ERA in seven appearances this month. Of the 36 hitters he had faced, 17 had reached base: six hits, a whopping nine walks, and two batters hit by pitches.
Immediately after Sandoval departed, though, Miller entered — and maybe figured it out. He turned in a perfect seventh on just eight pitches, getting a strikeout of David Fry, a routine fly out from Travis Bazzana, and a 108-miles-per-hour line out from Patrick Bailey.
The loss dropped the Red Sox to 85-74 and — with three games to go — ensured that they will not match their 89 wins from last year.
They totaled two hits. Nick Sogard and Jarren Duran each had a single. It was the fourth game this month in which the Sox recorded four hits or fewer.
Lefthander Ranger Suarez finished a strong September — and strong regular season — with five innings of one-run ball. He held the Guardians to three hits and a walk and struck out five.
Cleveland’s lone run against him came on Martínez’s home run, tucked inside the Pesky Pole, an estimated 319 feet down the right-field line. It came off his bat at only 94 m.p.h. The batted ball had an expected batting average of .160.
At the end of the first season of a five-year, $130 million contract, Suarez owns a 3.22 ERA, third best in the Red Sox’ rotation behind righthander Sonny Gray (2.72) and lefthander Payton Tolle (3.03).
Suarez suffered from a midseason dip — a groin injury followed by mediocrity — but rebounded late, posting a 1.09 ERA over his final four starts.
The Sox mustered minimal offense against opener Daniel Espino (perfect first inning with two strikeouts) and lefthander Joey Cantillo (one hit and no runs in five innings).
For Cantillo, who entered the night with the most walks in the American League (79) but issued just two free passes against the Red Sox, it was his third consecutive scoreless appearance. In all three, he entered behind an opener.

The Boston Red Sox hope to shift some momentum in advance of the playoffs when they host the Cleveland Guardians on Wednesday night in the second game of a three-game series.
Cleveland extended its winning streak to six games by beating Boston 3-2 on Tuesday. It was the third straight loss for the Red Sox (84-73), who have dropped eight of their last 12 games and own a 9-10 record in September but still clinched a wild-card berth on Sunday.Add left-handed reliever Erik Miller to the list of Boston's concerns as the Red Sox prepare for the playoffs. Miller looked sharp when the Red Sox acquired him from San Francisco in August, but he has allowed nine walks and hit two batters in September.One of those hit batsmen scored the game-winning run Tuesday. Miller hit Chase DeLauter to start the ninth inning, and DeLauter ended up breaking a 2-2 tie when he scored on Nathaniel Lowe's sacrifice fly.Miller has given up six runs and six walks in his past 3 1/3 innings and took the loss on Tuesday.'He's working through stuff,' Boston manager Chad Tracy said. 'I thought today was another step in the right direction. The hit batter ... the free passes are what gets you, and I think he also got some bad batted ball (luck). ... We're gonna try to get him out there a couple more times this week. Obviously still trust the stuff. If we can get that right, trust the stuff and his ability to strike out guys.'
Tuesday's win allowed the Guardians (82-75) to remain one game ahead of the Chicago White Sox at the top of the American League Central standings. Chicago has the division tiebreaker over Cleveland, which has a magic number of two to clinch a playoff berth.
Meanwhile, Guardians manager Stephen Vogt called Lowe 'a professional hitter.'
'You know he's not trying to do too much,' Vogt said. 'He's not going up there trying to be a hero, hitting a three-run homer. Just score the guy from third. Got a pitch up in the zone, and was able to drive it deep enough to left. And you know he continues to just make plays for us.'The Guardians won despite stranding 15 runners and a 1-for-12 hitting performance with runners in scoring position.'Again, felt like it was another night where we get a ton of traffic, we put a lot of pressure on, and just weren't able to get the big hit,' Vogt said. 'You know, we were able to get a couple runs across, but we left a lot on the table. But I just love the way we're making guys work. We're getting on base ... and we're going to come through a lot more often than not. And again, our pitching just picked us up again tonight.'Tracy said he expects center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (quadriceps) to be activated from the injured list on Wednesday. The manager also said first baseman Willson Contreras still has some soreness in his hand and won't be in the lineup Wednesday but is close to returning.Right-hander Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.82 ERA) will start for the Red Sox on Wednesday. He's 8-5 with a 3.12 ERA in 21 career starts against the Guardians. On May 30, he gave up one run on four hits and three walks over six innings against them. He struck out seven in a 9-1 win.Left-hander Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67 ERA) will start for Cleveland on Wednesday. It will be his first career appearance against the Red Sox.--Field Level Media

The Boston Red Sox clinched their second consecutive playoff berth Sunday and their third since 2021.
It was a season with the highest of highs and the lowest of lows in Boston as they started the season 10-17 before firing longtime manager Alex Cora.
In June, the Red Sox found themselves 14 games under .500 at a record of 32-46. This is when everything changed.
They swept the New York Yankees before losing two out of three games to the Washington Nationals.
The Red Sox went on the road and swept the Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and New York Mets to sit at 46-48 heading into the all-star break.
After nine straight road wins, the Red Sox headed home to face the 56-38 Tampa Bay Rays. Tampa has had Boston’s number in the past few seasons, but this weekend was different.
In the first game of a doubleheader after the break, the Red Sox took care of business 10-0. Then in the night cap, Tampa Bay Rays took an early 2-0 before outfielder Wilyer Abreu decided the next 24 hours were all about him. He hit two home runs on the way to a 5-3 Red Sox win.
The next game was the defining game of the winning streak. The Rays were matching the Sox in scoring all-game before Abreu stepped to the plate down 6-5 in the seventh. Abreu crushed a two-run homer to right field, sending himself and Fenway Park into a frenzy. His fourth home run in 24 hours put Boston up 7-6, a lead they would hold for 12 consecutive wins.
They swept Tampa the next day before taking the first two games of the series versus the Orioles to tie a franchise record 15 straight wins. That first win did not come without drama. A back-and-forth game was knotted up in the eighth when Caleb Durbin smacked a game winning homerun to left field. The “Durbinator” had a rough start to the season but became one of the centerpieces of this win streak.
The streak would end at 15 but just a week later, Boston would rip off another nine straight wins. Durbin hit a walk-off single in an instant classic 12-11 victory against the White Sox. Ceddanne Rafaela became the king of LA for a few days after smacking four home runs in three games against the back-to-back champs.
So here we are, the Red Sox are 84-72 with a firm grip on the second wild card spot in the American League. Now, the New York Yankees stand in their way.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox 2-1 in the three-game wildcard series last year, and Boston is looking for revenge this season.
The pitching will be the key for both teams. Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez will toe the rubber for Boston against the Yankees’ Gerritt Cole, Max Fried and Massachusetts’ own Cam Schlittler in the series.
In his first full season in the MLB, Tolle hit his stride. The southpaw posted a 3.02 ERA and a 10.4 K/9. He is also peaking at the right time, sporting a 0.75 ERA in two starts during September.
In a complete 180 from Tolle, Gray has been dominant in what may be his swan song in the majors. After being acquired via trade in the offseason, Gray has won 17 games, a career high for the veteran. He pitched 7.1 innings of one hit baseball while striking out nine in a June win over the Yankees.
Suarez signed a 5-year $130 million dollar contract with Boston in the offseason and has been solid as a member of the Sox. However, the 2026 all-star struggled in all three of his starts against the Yankees. The Bronx Bombers were 3-0 against Suarez.
Despite great performances by the Yankees, Suarez is a playoff pitcher. He had a 1.48 ERA in 42.2 postseason innings as a member of the Philadelphia Phillies. In Philadelphia’s 2022 run to the World Series, the Phillies won all five games Suarez pitched in. He only allowed two earned runs in 14.2 innings pitched in 2022.
Along with the starters, the back of the bullpen has been nails for Boston. Erik Miller, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman handled the seventh, eighth and ninth innings for interim manager Chad Tracy and the Red Sox. Miller came over at the trade deadline and did not allow an earned run in his first 10 appearances. Whitlock has been a staple in the Red Sox bullpen since 2021 and is possibly having his best year yet. He has a 1.75 ERA in 53 appearances. Chapman continues to age like fine wine. The 38-year-old was named an all-star for the second straight year and is 34/36 in save situations this year.
The rest of the hitters for the Red Sox will need to do some heavy lifting if they want to compete with the Yankees. Boston acquired Adley Rutschman at the deadline, and the catcher will be required to switch hit and catch in the playoffs. Wilson Contreras and Trevor Story will add postseason experience to the lineup while former top prospect Roman Anthony and local legend Mickey Gasper will look to provide during their first playoff at bats.
If the standings hold, the Red Sox and Yankees will battle in the Bronx on Tuesday for the wildcard series, a statement no Red Sox fan would have believed in June.

The final week of the MLB season always features plenty of altered and adjusted pitching plans.
Normally the one consistent throughout the drumbeat of the 162-game MLB season is a team’s pitching plan; regardless of whether a team has an ace on the mound or is going with pitching madness, the goal is always to get the best position to win while taking it a day at a time.
But that's a bit different this week.
While some teams are playing out the string and giving their starters one last opportunity to pitch before drifting off into the winter, the teams that have already clinched are stuck in the limbo of trying to cover the now while also preparing for the postseason.
It’s not like football or basketball where you can just throw random backups out there. Every inning needs to be covered, and there’s only so many innings you can give to pitchers who aren’t a part of your postseason plans.
Even if the Guardians won’t be in that position for a couple days (even if they clinch a postseason spot later today the American League Central race still won’t be settled, the Boston Red Sox's already know their postseason fate by virtue of being all but locked into the American League’s No. 5 seed.
We got an early example of how that could change their pitching plans on Monday when manager Andy Tracy pulled budding ace Peyton Tolle after five innings, and we got another example of it later in the game whenTracy went to Erik Miller in the ninth inning of a tied game instead of going to Aroldis Chapman… and Miller gave up the go-ahead run on a Nathaniel Lowe sacrifice fly.
The Red Sox are already playing with their postseason plans in mind, and those plans just got a bit more convoluted thanks to Miller’s rough outing.
The Red sox's bullpen struggles could help the Guardians in their quest to make the postseason
While Miller has largely been excellent since the Red Sox acquired him in August, he’s now allowed a run in three straight appearances and seems to be falling down manager Andy Tracy’s trust tree.
Miller opened his outing by hitting Chase DeLauter on the forearm with a pitch before surrendering a single to Jo Adell that was followed by Lowe’s sacrifice fly.
After the game, Tracy said that Miller was “working through some things,” which was obvious to everyone in the ballpark and watching at home.
Those struggles set up what should be an interesting last two games at Fenway Park. The Sox have two of their best pitchers going in the final two games of the series (Sonny Gray today and Ranger Suarez tomorrow), and it’s hard to believe the Red Sox are going to give them a ton of run in either of their starts.
While the Guardians may not get a chance to benefit from Boston’s relief struggles in the postseason since Boston will likely be locked into the other side of the bracket, they can use it to their benefit over the next 48 hours as they work to nail down a postseason spot.

The regular season has come to an end for Boston Red Sox starting pitcher Payton Tolle. He made his final scheduled start on Tuesday night, throwing 5.2 innings and giving up 2 earned runs in a no decision against the Cleveland Guardians.
There was some reason for concern in the start, though. Tolle’s velocity was down. In the first inning, he was hitting around 97 mph on the radar gun. By the second, he was around 94 mph.
There were a couple of reasons being suggested, neither of which would be good. He could be dealing with the cold, which going into October isn’t what you want to hear. Or, he could have a mechanical issue, which leads to more questions for the young Red Sox pitcher. For his part, Tolle would blame his mechanics.
“I think there was a little bit of just trying to find my legs for a second,” Tolle said. “I think I got very nitpicky. I got trying to be too fine. It’s like, I don’t — you’re going to see the velo dip whenever I’m being too fine. That’s kind of what happened there, especially with those walks. Just trying too hard on some pitches.”
This comes at a time when Red Sox reliever Erik Miller is battling mechanical issues. Those are issues that have led to concerns about what he can be in the postseason. At the very least, Tolle seemed to figure it out midgame.
“So, it is what it is,” Tolle said. “But I think later I got back to just trying to fly through zone and let it be what it be.”
Boston Red Sox Fans Embraced Payton Tolle in 2026
Boston Red Sox fans got their first taste of Payton Tolle in 2025, but he was still a rookie who started 2026 in the minors. It wouldn’t be until injuries hit the rotation that Tolle made it back to the MLB team, which is a tough spot to be in for anyone. Still, he and the fanbase have seemed to embrace each other.
So, it was no surprise that the Fenway Faithful walked him off the mound on Tuesday with a standing ovation. Unless the Red Sox can win a playoff round, that was his final home game of the season.
Tolle wrapped up the regular season with a 3.03 ERA in 26 games and 148.2 innings. He also had a 1.096 WHIP and 10.4 strikeouts per nine. More importantly, he proved he has secondary pitches beyond his fastball, which is still his bread and butter.
Along the way, Red Sox fans embraced Tolle for how he plays the game. He’s both fiery and passionate, but he doesn’t take himself overly seriously. That has seen him hug runners to tag them out, do push-ups after slipping, and smile before throwing an immaculate inning.
The Red Sox Need Tolle for the Postseason
There is no doubt that the Red Sox are going to need Payton Tolle at his best for the postseason. The question is whether or not he’s getting the ball in Game 1. For his part, manager Chad Tracy didn’t want to give anything away just yet.
“TBD,” Tracy said on when Tolle will pitch next. “But good try, though.”
Tolle only got to pitch 0.1 innings last postseason. The Red Sox need more this year from him, and he’s excited for the opportunity.
“I’m excited… I’ll keep going back to how far we’ve come. Go back to June, and what we were thinking sitting in this same room in June. I’m just really proud of this group; this is incredible. I’ve had so much fun— obviously,” Tolle said.

The Boston Red Sox lost 3-2 to the Guardians on Tuesday night at Fenway Park. The game was tied heading into the ninth inning. It did not stay that way for long.
Erik Miller entered to protect the tie and hit Chase DeLauter to start the inning. Two batters later, Nathaniel Lowe lifted a sacrifice fly that brought DeLauter home with the go-ahead run. Miller threw 22 pitches. Ten were strikes. The Guardians had their lead, and the Red Sox had another loss.
It was the fourth consecutive outing in which Miller has allowed at least one run. After the game, the left-hander did not sugarcoat where things stand.
Miller’s Patience Is Running Thin
Miller was asked about his recent stretch and whether his patience with himself was wearing down. He did not dodge the question.
“It’s definitely running thin at this point,” Miller said. “I’d be lying if I said otherwise…I would like to have been through this by now, be over it.”
In September, Miller has posted an 8.53 ERA and a 2.37 WHIP. He has recorded one clean inning in seven appearances. For a pitcher who spent the summer as one of the most reliable left-handed setup arms in the American League, the slide has been sudden.
Miller said after the game that he has been working through a mechanical issue that he has not been able to shake. The frustration is compounded by the reality that the only way to fix it is to keep pitching in live situations. There is no shortcut. The regular season has five games left, and the postseason starts a week from Tuesday.
Tracy Still Believes in the Stuff
Manager Chad Tracy acknowledged the struggles but offered a different read on Tuesday’s outing.
“I thought today was even another step in the right direction,” Tracy said.
Tracy plans to get Miller into a couple more games before the regular season ends Sunday. The idea is to give him every opportunity to find the command before the Wild Card Series begins on September 29. Tracy said after the game that the trust in Miller’s raw ability has not changed, even as the results have gone sideways. The stuff is not the problem. The location is.
Final Word for the Red Sox
Erik Miller is not hiding from this. He knows the numbers. He knows the stakes. He is frustrated with himself and not pretending otherwise.
The stuff is still there. The command is not. Five days remain to find it.
Miller’s patience may be running thin. The Red Sox’ belief in him has not wavered. Whether those two things can meet in the middle before October will go a long way toward determining how far this team can go.

BOSTON — Nathaniel Lowe had a tiebreaking sacrifice fly off reliever Erik Miller in the ninth inning, and the Cleveland Guardians maintained their slim in the AL Central with a 3-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.
Angel Martínez had three hits for the Guardians, who entered the day with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the division. Chicago owns the tiebreaker by winning the season series. Cleveland stranded 15 baserunners.
The loss was Boston’s eighth in 12 games, spoiling Chad Tracy’s first game as manager after the club named him its 49th in team history.
Adley Rutschman added three hits for Boston, which clinched one of the AL’s wild-card spots on Sunday.
Boston pinch hitter Mickey Gasper hit Hunter Gaddis’ first pitch, tying it at 2-2 leading off the eighth.
Gaddis (5-3) got the win and Cade Smith recorded the final three outs for his 40th save.
Miller (4-2) hit a batter and gave up two hits in an inning.
A strong candidate for the AL Rookie of the Year, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick gave up a run over five innings. He lowered his ERA to 2.55 and is on pace to become the fourth rookie starting pitcher in MLB history with an ERA under 2.60 and averaging 9.0 or more strikeouts per nine innings.
In his tune-up for a likely playoff start next week, Boston lefty Payton Tolle struggled with his control over 5 2/3 innings, giving up two runs on eight hits.
Up next
Guardians LHP Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67 ERA) is set to face Red Sox RHP Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.82) on Wednesday in the middle game of the three-game series.

item.content:encoded:
In this purgatorial period for the Red Sox, after they clinched a playoff berth over the weekend and before they open the postseason next week, what matters?
The result Tuesday, a 3-2 loss to the Guardians at Fenway Park, was not of major significance.
Of greater note was the how — and what those trends may portend heading into the most important time of year: another ugly outing for reliever Erik Miller, and another night of minimal hitting for the lineup.
The Red Sox (84-73) have dropped three games in a row and eight of their past 12.
“We’ve still got five games to play, and you [have to] keep guys out there and engaged and ready to roll,” manager Chad Tracy said. “I told the guys before, we earned the right to be in position to be able to line things up. That being said, we still want to go out and win the games. We had a chance to tonight.”
Miller inherited a tied game in the ninth inning and struggled again, allowing a game-deciding run and throwing 22 pitches (10 strikes). He hit his first batter, Chase DeLauter, with a pitch. DeLauter eventually scored on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly. Altogether, Miller yielded two hits and a walk.
In September, the Sox’ theoretical top lefthanded setup man has one clean inning in seven attempts, a 8.53 ERA, and a 2.37 WHIP.
Miller said his patience with himself — and a mechanical issue he is trying to fix — is “definitely running thin at this point.”
“I’d be lying if I say otherwise,” he said. “I would like to have been through this by now, be over it. But … there’s no way I can feel better and work through it without throwing [in] a game. So that’s just how it’s going to have to be: keep throwing, get through it.”
Tracy, noting that Miller will pitch in a couple more games before the regular season ends Sunday, added: “I thought today was even another step in the right direction.”
Offensively, the Red Sox had few highlights. Mickey Gasper launched a pinch-hit tying home run off setup man Hunter Gaddis to lead off the eighth, but the Sox totaled nine runners stranded on base and went 0 for 9 with men in scoring position.
In the positives column: Adley Rutschman finished 3 for 4, with two doubles (and a line out to deep center) coming against lefthanders.
Entering the game, Rutschman was 2 for 26 with no extra-base hits against lefties as a member of the Red Sox.
“Being a switch hitter has a lot that goes into it, and you go through phases where you’re hitting good [from] one side and not the other and it flip flops sometimes and then goes back,” Rutschman said. “I want to be in a good spot, especially with the playoffs coming up.”
In a matchup between perhaps the top two rookie pitchers this year, Payton Tolle (5⅔ innings, two runs) was almost equal to fellow lefthander Parker Messick (five innings, one run) of the Guardians.
Tolle slogged through a 22-pitch second frame, during which he allowed three hits and two walks but managed to hold the AL Central-leading Guardians (82-75) to the two runs.
When Tracy pulled him in the sixth, Tolle walked off the Fenway mound — for potentially the last time this year — to a standing ovation from the fans behind the home dugout. He waved back to them.
“I think he’s won them over pretty significantly,” Tracy said.
Tolle finished his rookie season with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148⅔ innings (26 starts).
Up next: a start in the AL Wild Card Series.
“It’s the postseason. This is what we play for,” Tolle said. “But it is what it is. We go on, and we have a job to do.”

For all intents and purposes, none of these last games down the stretch mean anything to the Red Sox. They have already punched their ticket to the playoffs and nothing that happens from here on out will change that.
But while readying themselves for the games that matter, the Red Sox would still prefer to go into the postseason with some momentum, and Tuesday’s performance was at times pretty hard to watch.
Playing without three projected postseason starters, the Red Sox suffered a listless 3-2 loss in their series opener against the Cleveland Guardians. Despite a game-tying pinch hit home run by Mickey Gasper in the bottom of the eighth, the Red Sox gave the lead right back in the ninth, capping off a night riddled with poor decisions and uncharacteristic mistakes.
Reliever Erik Miller saw his struggles continue by allowing two hits, a walk, a hit batsman and the go-ahead sacrifice fly by Angel Martinez in the top of the ninth, and outside of Gasper and Adley Rutschman going 3 for 4 with two doubles and a run scored, there wasn’t much to write home about as the Red Sox suffered their third straight defeat.
Making his final start before the playoffs, Payton Tolle wasn’t as sharp as he would’ve hoped, but once again he gave the Red Sox a chance to win.
After posting a scoreless first, Tolle allowed two runs and five baserunners over the course of a challenging second inning. He started by giving up a leadoff double, had a soft grounder from David Fry deflect off his leg and into the outfield for an RBI single, and allowed another single and a walk to load the bases with nobody out.
Tolle was able to minimize the damage from there, allowing a second run to score on a double play ball by Brayan Rocchio before escaping the inning. He continued facing traffic for the rest of his outing but grinded his way into the sixth and departed to a standing ovation from the Fenway Park faithful.
Tolle finished with two runs allowed on eight hits, two walks and a hit batsman over 5 2/3 innings with five strikeouts. He fell one out short of recording another quality start, leaving him with 13 in 26 outings, and he ends his rookie year with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.
The Red Sox got a run back in the bottom of the second after Adley Rutschman led off with a double and came around to score on an RBI groundout by Andruw Monasterio, but otherwise the bats struggled against Guardians rookie Parker Messick. The left-hander, who came into the game with a 2.57 ERA and projects as a possible AL Cy Young Award finalist, limited the Red Sox to one run on five hits over five innings.
One thing Boston was able to do was drive up the rookie’s pitch count, particularly in the fourth when Monasterio was able to work a 12-pitch walk. That helped force the lefty from the game after five, giving the Red Sox a chance to try their luck against Cleveland’s bullpen.
The Red Sox let a golden opportunity go to waste in the bottom of the sixth, leaving men at second and third, but Alec Gamboa kept it a one-run game in the top of the seventh despite the Guardians taking advantage of some sloppy baseball to get runners at second and third themselves with one out.
Cleveland’s Fry, who had already grounded into a fielder’s choice where the runner was thrown out at the plate earlier in the third inning, did so a second time for the second out of the seventh, and Gamboa struck out former No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana to end the inning.
Then, in the bottom of the eighth, Gasper struck for his 10th home run of the season, hitting the first pitch he saw from Guardians reliever Hunter Gaddis 390 feet to the right field stands.
The good vibes didn’t last long.
Miller, who had proven an impactful bullpen addition since his arrival at the trade deadline, saw his recent control issues continue with his latest ugly outing. The left-hander hit the first batter he faced, gave up the lead on a sacrifice fly by Martinez and eventually loaded the bases before getting a fly out to keep things from spiraling further.
Miller has now allowed six runs and six walks over his past 3 1/3 innings, a trend the Red Sox can’t afford to continue if he’s to remain a high-leverage option in the playoffs.

The Craig Breslow era in Boston has felt like a roller coaster ride. Hired at the start of the 2023-24 offseason, the Boston Red Sox have not had a losing season under Breslow, despite wild swings in the team's form over the three years.
With the Red Sox clinching a playoff berth for the second year in a row, team ownership decided that now was the time to exercise two options on their Chief Baseball Officer's contract, guaranteeing his deal for the 2029 and 2030 seasons. On the surface, a head of baseball operations who got his team to the playoffs in years two and three of their time running the club getting years added to their contract, would make sense, but in Breslow's case it isn't as straightforward.
It was only three months ago when most of Red Sox Nation was calling for Breslow's head. The Red Sox were 32-46 on June 24, dead last in the division, and it already seemed like the season was over. It took a miraculous turnaround to get the team to the playoffs. Not to say that Breslow had nothing to do with that; he had added a lot of players to the roster who were key contributors, but that has a lot more to do with the players and coaches than the front office.
Breslow's tenure has also been marred by controversy, specifically the Rafael Devers drama. It was his handling of the situation, along with former manager Alex Cora, that ultimately led to the fracture of the relationship with the team's then-face of the franchise. While the fanbase was split on whose side they took, player or team, his actions after the fact didn't make it any better.
Red Sox's Craig Breslow had the hottest seat of any GM only three months ago
It was the signing of Alex Bregman that caused the Devers drama in the first place. While Breslow was praised for the signing, Bregman opted out at the end of the year and was then not re-signed. The Red Sox went from two elite third basemen to none in the span of a season. It wasn't a good look for the Red Sox CBO.
Now, Breslow's pivot from all of the drama and mess surrounding Devers and Bregman looks incredibly good in hindsight. The additions of Ranger Suarez, Sonny Gray, Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and others have been extremely impactful to the Red Sox's success this season. While some of those moves were celebrated at the time they happened, others like the Durbin-Kyle Harrison swap (that also netted the Red Sox Andruw Monasterio and Anthony Seigler) were heavily scrutinized.
Breslow also made good moves at the trade deadline, adding Erik Miller and Eli White, who have looked good for the Sox. He also made the splash trade for Adley Rutschman, which hasn't worked as well on the field, but certainly instilled confidence in the team, knowing the front office believed in them.
Red Sox could've softened the impact by extending one of Craig Breslow's options at first
All of this is to say that Breslow's time as CBO hasn't been as smooth sailing as the records would suggest. He has had some high highs but also some low lows. Why did ownership feel the need to exercise both options right now? The first option wasn't needed until the 2029 season, two years out. The second was for 2030, three years out.
Doing the first one now would've been fine — picking up the 2029 option gives Breslow another three comfortable seasons on his contract. That would make him more comfortable making moves for the future and give him the job security to know he will likely be in place to see them play out. Selecting the 2030 option on the same day was unnecessary, though.
There have been too many hiccups in the three years under Breslow to say he has warranted another four seasons. The start of 2026 could easily repeat itself in 2027. Should ownership feel the need to relieve him of his duties early, then this makes it that much harder. Breslow hasn't won a World Series in Boston; in fact, he hasn't even made it out of the Wild Card round. Exercising the option for 2030 feels very premature.
Breslow has not done a bad job in Boston. At the end of the day, it's results that matter, and Breslow's teams have made the playoffs two out of three times. He shouldn't be fearing for his job, but his contract also wasn't ending for another two seasons. It feels early to be handing him the keys so far down the road after the drama of his first two years as CBO.

SAN FRANCISCO — First, the good news: outfielder Bo Davidson and infielder Marcelo Mayer will make their long-awaited Giants debuts on Monday night at Oracle Park against the Minnesota Twins. Now, the bad: Bryce Eldridge and Jung Hoo Lee became the latest players to hit the injured list.
Mayer, acquired at the trade deadline from the Boston Red Sox, was reinstated from the injured list, while Davidson was called up from Triple-A Sacramento. Davidson will play right field and bat third in his major-league debut, while Mayer will bat fourth and be the team’s designated hitter.
“Just showing them what I can do and giving them the best I can every game until the season’s over,” Davidson said when asked what he could provide. “Just showing them what Bo is.”
What is Bo?
“You’ll see,” Davidson said with a smile.
Meanwhile, Eldridge landed on the seven-day concussion list after bumping his head at the team’s hotel in Los Angeles, while Lee landed on the 10-day injured list with a groin contusion after fouling a ball off himself on Sunday. Lee’s season is over, and manager Tony Vitello said he doesn’t anticipate Eldridge will play again this season, which ends Sunday.
With Lee landing on the injured list, every member of the Opening Day lineup is either on the injured list (Lee, Willy Adames, Rafael Devers, Matt Chapman, Logan Webb, Casey Schmitt, Harrison Bader) or has been traded (Patrick Bailey, Heliot Ramos, Luis Arraez). The only players from the Opening Day roster still on the roster are infielder Christian Koss and right-hander Landen Roupp.
Adames (left elbow sprain) took grounders and batting practice on Monday afternoon, but he’s very unlikely to return before the end of the season.
Eldridge, who will turn 22 next month, exceeded expectations as a rookie and should be a foundational piece of the Giants’ lineup alongside Devers. Over 107 games, Eldridge hit .269/.364/.461 with 17 home runs, 23 doubles and 57 RBIs. Among rookies, Eldridge’s 130 wRC+ (weighted runs created plus) was the third-highest in the majors.
“Incredibly impressive,” Vitello said of Eldridge’s season. “We summarized that a little bit with him this morning in there. Maturity is the word that gets thrown around a bunch, but it got thrown around in there, too. I think consistency is the other word. He attached that to himself in a good way, not in a braggadocious way.
“If I could speak for him through his own words, a big difference between last year and this year is understanding the ups and downs and how to maintain consistency, which is a lot easier to formulate or plan out than it is to put into act.”
Along with the offense, Vitello also highlighted Eldridge’s defense, which was his biggest question as a prospect. After committing 18 errors in 2024 and 9 in 2025, Eldridge only had two errors this season in the majors and minors. Eldridge also graded out well by Baseball Savant’s new first baseman receiving metric.
Going into next season, one area where Vitello believes Eldridge can improve is baserunning.
“He’s got good instincts, but there’s so many things that he’s seeing for the first time in his life, literally,” Vitello said. “Safety bunts, stuff like that. And then on the base running … he didn’t do anything that would cause us to jump here in the dugout or cost us big, but for a guy that’s going to be on base as often as he is — and he’s not a burner — he’s got to be good on those little separators of reads, preparation before a pitch.”
Davidson, 24, is the Giants’ No. 5 prospect, per Baseball America. Over 125 games this season with Double-A Richmond and Triple-A Sacramento, Davidson hit .290 with 29 home runs, 20 steals and 94 RBIs. He was a candidate to get called up earlier this month but missed a week after fouling a ball off his foot on Sept. 9.
For all of Davidson’s production on the field, he believes the biggest area he’s grown has been “being a better man off the field.”
Davidson is one of many intriguing prospects in a farm system that has climbed the rankings. Along with Davidson, the Giants’ farm system is headlined by shortstops Josuar Gonzalez and Luis Hernandez, as well as right-handed pitcher Jackson Flora.
“We’ve got a very special group of guys that’s coming through,” said Davidson, whose mother, brother, girlfriend and daughter will be in attendance. “The farm itself, the numbers this year just showed. Us being really good brothers off the field, it just shows on the field with the chemistry.”
“I’m excited to see Bo again,” Vitello said. “Just kind of knowing who he was in high school and junior college. … We were able to get him some action in spring training, and then you’re following along, following along. We knew [his promotion] would happen at some point.”
Mayer, 23, was traded to the Giants on Aug. 3 from the Boston Red Sox in exchange for lefty reliever Erik Miller and minor-league outfielder Carlos Gutierrez. The infielder had been recovering from a bone stress reaction to the left ulna, as well as a bone bruise on his right foot.
Vitello anticipates Mayer will primarily be the team’s designated hitter over the final six games, but he could also see some time in the infield.

The San Francisco Giants are down to two members of their Opening Day roster still active with the club after placing first baseman Bryce Eldridge and right fielder Jung Hoo Lee on the injured list Monday.
Eldridge landed on the seven-day concussion injured list after getting hurt in the team's Los Angeles hotel on Friday, according to the team. He didn't play in the series as the Dodgers swept three games.
His IL move is retroactive to Friday, leaving open the possibility he could return to action before the season ends this weekend, but manager Tony Vitello told reporters that Eldridge likely will be shut down for the rest of the campaign.
Lee was placed on the 10-day IL due to a groin contusion, so his season is over. He exited San Francisco's 3-1 loss to the Dodgers on Sunday in the seventh inning, an inning after fouling a pitch off his groin.
Right-hander Landen Roupp and shortstop Christian Koss are the last players on the Giants' active roster who were with the team when the season started, though neither was in the lineup on March 25 against the New York Yankees. Many of the other players from the season-opening roster were either part of the team's sell-off at the trade deadline or are on the IL.
Eldridge, 21, has a .269 batting average, a .364 on-base percentage and a .461 slugging percentage with 17 homers and 57 RBIs in 107 games this year. He began his major league career with San Francisco in 2025, hitting .107 with no homers in 10 games.
Lee, 28, batting .276/.320/.404 with 10 home runs and 57 RBIs in 143 games this season. Through three years with the Giants, he has a .270/.322/.397 batting line with 20 homers and 120 RBIs over 330 games.
The Giants filled the two roster vacancies by activating infielder Marcelo Mayer from the injured list and promoting outfielder Bo Davidson from Triple-A Sacramento.
Mayer, 23, hasn't played a major league game since late June due to left arm and right foot injuries. The Giants acquired him from the Boston Red Sox on Aug. 3 in exchange for left-hander Erik Miller, and Mayer played four games for Sacramento in mid-August before he was shut down again.
Davidson, 24, split the minor league season between Double-A Richmond and Sacramento, batting a combined .290/.361/.527 with 29 homers, 94 RBIs and 20 stolen bases in 125 games.
Both newcomers immediately joined San Francisco's starting lineup Monday night against the visiting Minnesota Twins. Davidson, playing right field and batting third, hit a first-inning single in his initial major league at-bat. Mayer served as the designated hitter and was slotted into the cleanup spot.
Left-hander Philip Abner was for assignment to clear a spot for Davidson on the 40-man roster. Abner, 24, had no decisions and a 9.64 ERA in five appearances for the Giants this year before he was optioned to Sacramento on Sunday. He pitched for the Los Angeles Angels earlier this season.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have officially clinched a postseason berth, completing one of the most improbable turnarounds in MLB history.
But the real test begins next week. After falling to the New York Yankees in last year’s Wild Card Series, Boston is looking to make a deeper October run this time around, and it looks like the Yankees will once again stand in the way.
It’s been a total team effort for Boston all season long, but the playoffs are where stars emerge and the margin for error becomes razor thin. While nearly everyone on the postseason roster will play a role, we’ve narrowed it down to the 10 players who could have the biggest impact on how far this team goes.
Here are the 10 most important -- not necessarily the best -- Red Sox players for the 2026 playoffs:
1. Payton Tolle, SP
What a difference a year makes. Last year, Tolle experienced growing pains in his first MLB stint and pitched just 1/3 of an inning in the Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. This time, he's coming off an exceptional rookie campaign with a chance to start Game 1 in the Bronx.
Tolle will enter the postseason with momentum on his side. The 23-year-old tallied 12 strikeouts while allowing just one run in six innings against Baltimore. He followed that up with six shutout innings against Kansas City, including an immaculate inning to begin the game.
If Tolle continues to perform at this level, he'll give the Red Sox another frontline starter who can match up against other teams' aces. He's the pitcher with the greatest opportunity to change the trajectory of this postseason roster.
If the Red Sox make a deep postseason run, it'll be because their rookie left-hander delivered each time he took the mound on the big stage.
2. Sonny Gray, SP
We're sticking with pitching, because pitching is what propelled this Red Sox club to a postseason berth in the first place.
If Tolle is No. 1, it would be silly not to put Gray right behind him at No. 2. The 36-year-old veteran stabilized the rotation in the wake of Garrett Crochet's injury. He was signed to be the No. 3 starter behind Crochet and Ranger Suarez, but he performed like an ace with a 17-5 record and a 2.82 ERA in 28 starts.
Now, Boston will lean on Gray and his big-game experience to lead the staff in October. Even if he doesn't start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, Gray will play a huge role in any postseason success.
3. Roman Anthony, LF/DH
The top position player on our list is the 22-year-old many expected to anchor Boston's lineup and produce an MVP-caliber season in 2026. Instead, Anthony spent most of the year on the injured list and has largely struggled in the 50 games he's been healthy. We know what the former No. 1 prospect is capable of, however, and he'll significantly raise the Red Sox' ceiling if he plays up to his potential in the postseason.
The Red Sox will lean heavily on their pitching staff throughout the playoffs, but Anthony is the X-factor in the lineup. This is a completely different club when he gets hot.
All it will take is a signature postseason moment for Red Sox fans to forget about the disappointing start to Anthony's young career.
4. Ranger Suarez, SP
OK, back to pitching. A big reason the Red Sox signed Suarez to a five-year, $130 million contract in free agency is that he has a stellar postseason track record. The 31-year-old boasts a 1.48 ERA across 11 playoff appearances (eight starts) with the Philadelphia Phillies.
The only reason he isn't higher on this list is we project him to be the No. 3 starter, which means we won't even see him if the Sox get swept out of the Wild Card Series. If Boston advances, another strong postseason from Suarez will be critical for their World Series chances.
5. Wilyer Abreu, RF
Abreu is one of Boston's best all-around players, but he's a streaky hitter. The Red Sox' mediocre offense can't afford for him to go cold in the postseason, so he's an incredibly important piece if they hope to make a deep run.
When he's hot, Abreu's bat is elite. He leads the American League with 36 doubles along with 24 homers in 151 games.
As important as his bat will be, Abreu's Gold Glove defense in right field will also be a difference-maker. Postseason games can come down to one defensive miscue, and Abreu has earned a reputation as one of the best defensive right fielders in baseball.
If Abreu can give the Red Sox consistent at-bats and quality defense, he can quietly become one of the most impactful players on the roster over an entire series.
6. Willson Contreras, 1B
We've got the Venezuelan sluggers back-to-back. Contreras has been the Red Sox' most consistent bat all season, and he'll be leaned on heavily in the heart of the lineup throughout the playoffs.
Unlike most of Boston's lineup, Contreras will enter the Wild Card Series with plenty of postseason experience. He won a World Series with the 2016 Chicago Cubs and has 30 playoff games under his belt in total.
With a team-high 27 homers, Contreras will be counted on to supply the Red Sox lineup with power throughout their playoff run. If he goes cold, there will be even more pressure on guys like Anthony, Abreu, and the player who's next up on our list to get runs on the board.
7. Adley Rutschman, C
Rutschman will need to step it up offensively, but his importance goes beyond his bat because of his position. One could argue the role he plays behind the plate is even more crucial.
As Boston's starting catcher, Rutschman will be responsible for managing the pitching staff through almost every postseason game, meaning he'll be involved on almost every pitch thrown. There's also a significant downgrade at catcher if he goes down with an injury, with only Connor Wong and Mickey Gasper as his potential backups.
For the Red Sox to make it far, Rutschman has to be more than just a productive hitter; he must also work seamlessly with the rotation and bullpen while living up to his reputation as one of the best defensive backstops in the league.
8. Aroldis Chapman, CP
Having a closer who can slam the door shut gives clubs a huge advantage come postseason time. The Red Sox are fortunate to have arguably the best of the bunch.
While Chapman wasn't otherworldly in 2026 like he was in 2025, he still was elite with a 1.95 ERA in 52 appearances. He'll look to limit free passes after watching his walk rate jump from 2.2 to 4.1 BB/9 over last year. If he does that, Boston can effectively shorten games by having him available for the ninth inning. He can also single-handedly lose games, automatically making him one of the club's most important players for the postseason.
9. Garrett Whitlock, RP
Boston's bullpen is perhaps its biggest strength heading into the postseason, and that's because of the Whitlock/Chapman combo at the back end. Whitlock has been an elite set-up man with a 1.75 ERA and 0.877 WHIP across 53 appearances this season.
Starters typically have shorter outings in the playoffs, so we could see the Red Sox turn to Whitlock early and often throughout October if they advance past the Wild Card Series. He's the reliever Boston will count on to mow down the heart of an opposing lineup in a high-leverage situation. That could be the difference between a win and a loss, and that's why Whitlock makes the top 10 over some other very important players.
10. Ceddanne Rafaela, CF
Rafaela rounds out our top 10 most important Red Sox players for the postseason, but don't let his ranking fool you. With elite defense in center field and a bat that made a significant leap this season, he can be considered another X-factor for this club in the playoffs.
If Boston makes a deep run, there's a good chance we'll get at least one signature Rafaela moment. The 26-year-old has a knack for coming up big in the clutch, whether it's with a timely extra-base hit or a mind-blowing catch in center field.
Rafaela's glaring absence during his time on the injured list with a quad injury has highlighted his importance to this club. If he's back to full strength in time for the playoffs, that'll give the Red Sox a major boost.
Honorable mentions: 3B Caleb Durbin, SS Trevor Story, LF/DH Jarren Duran, RP Erik Miller, RP Tyron Guerrero, P Brayan Bello and P Jake Bennett.
They didn't crack the top 10, but that doesn't mean they won't have huge roles in October.
Durbin completely changes the outlook of the offense when he's hitting. He's also been an elite defensive third baseman all season long.
Story has been one of Boston's best hitters since returning from the injured list. There's no guarantee that'll carry over into the playoffs, but he'll at least have to be adequate defensively as the team's starting shortstop.
Duran had a 2026 to forget, and with Anthony in left field and Mickey Gasper likely at DH, he'll probably spend a fair amount of time on the bench. Still, he's the type of player who can change a game with one swing, and his speed is a huge factor.
Miller and Guerrero will have major roles at the back end of the bullpen. Bello (if he makes the roster) and Bennett will be leaned on as bulk relievers. Miller has struggled lately, Guerrero is returning from injury, Bello is unproven in the playoffs, and we haven't seen Bennett come out of the 'pen.
